# Prologue: One loan, two answers.

On 11 April 2024, at 10.00am, the Court of Appeal handed down a judgment remotely. Its front page records the time. The case was *BlackRock HoldCo 5, LLC v HMRC* [2024] EWCA Civ 330.

The case was about one set of loans, worth about $4bn, made inside one group of companies. Two rules of UK corporation tax looked at those loans. The first rule asked what strangers would have done, and it found nothing wrong. The second rule asked why the borrower had borrowed, and it took away every pound of the interest deductions. The taxpayer won the first argument and lost the case.

This prologue tells that story and then stops. It opens a book written for the CTA Advanced Technical paper, **Taxation of Larger Companies and Groups**. The law throughout is the law for **FY2026** (1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027). You met the basic loan relationship rules, and group relief, in *The Living Law* (TKS), chapters 21 and 24. Here the same rules meet a group on a far larger scale.

## A British link in an American chain.

In 2009 the BlackRock group bought the business of Barclays Global Investors. Part of the money for that acquisition travelled down a chain of companies formed in Delaware. Each was a limited liability company, and the judgments number them like stepping stones. The one that matters is **LLC5**.

LLC5 was a Delaware company. But it was managed and controlled in the UK, so for corporation tax it was a UK-resident company. Its US parent, **LLC4**, put cash and shares into it. In return LLC4 took common shares and **loan notes of about $4bn**. LLC5 then put the money and shares into the next company down the chain, **LLC6**, and took **preference shares**. LLC6 used the funds towards the purchase.

| Step | Who | What moved | UK tax result for LLC5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | LLC4 → LLC5 | Cash and shares in; LLC5 issues common shares and ~$4bn loan notes | Interest on the notes: loan relationship debits (CTA 2009 Part 5) |
| 2 | LLC5 → LLC6 | Cash and shares in; LLC6 issues preference shares to LLC5 | Preference dividends: exempt |
| 3 | LLC6 | Funds used towards the acquisition | — |
| 4 | LLC5 → UK group companies | Non-trading deficit surrendered as group relief, for no payment | Deficit used against other UK companies' profits |

Picture the chain as a sandwich: American bread on top, American bread underneath, and one British filling in the middle. The filling had a very particular taste.

Look at LLC5's tax position. Its income was the dividends on its preference shares, and those dividends were **exempt** from UK tax. Its expense was the interest on the loan notes, a deductible **debit** under the loan relationship rules. So each year LLC5 had no taxable income and a large non-trading deficit. It surrendered that deficit, as **group relief**, to other BlackRock companies in the UK, without asking for payment.

Commentators put the deductions claimed at about **£654m** (Macfarlanes; Bloomberg Tax). HMRC refused them on two grounds: **transfer pricing** and the **unallowable purpose rule**. The case climbed through three courts. On each rule the answer changed at least once.

| Court | Date and judges | Transfer pricing | Unallowable purpose | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| First-tier Tribunal, [2020] UKFTT 443 (TC) | 3 November 2020; Judge John Brooks | Taxpayer: an independent lender would have lent the same amount on the same interest terms, with covenants that would have been given | Two main purposes (commercial and tax), but all debits apportioned to the commercial purpose | Taxpayer wins |
| Upper Tribunal, [2022] UKUT 199 (TCC) | 19 July 2022; Michael Green J and Judge Rupert Jones | HMRC: covenants absent from the actual deal could not be imported | HMRC: the commercial benefit a by-product of a tax-driven decision; all debits to the tax purpose | HMRC wins |
| Court of Appeal, [2024] EWCA Civ 330 | 11 April 2024 (heard 5–6 March 2024); Peter Jackson, Nugee and Falk LJJ (main judgment Falk LJ) | **Taxpayer**: FTT's finding restored | **HMRC**: tax-advantage main purpose; all debits attributable to it | **HMRC wins** |
| Supreme Court | Permission refused (Lord Hodge, Lord Hamblen, Lady Simler); "does not raise an arguable point of law"; list dated 13 October 2024 | — | — | CA decision stands |

## What strangers would have done.

Start with transfer pricing. The rules now live in **TIOPA 2010 Part 4**. They apply where provision is made between two connected persons (the participation condition) on terms that differ from the **arm's length provision**. If the actual provision gives one of them a potential UK tax advantage, that person's profits are computed as if the arm's length provision had been made (s 147). The arm's length provision can even be **no provision at all**, where strangers would never have dealt (s 151(2)).

HMRC argued exactly that: no independent lender would have lent $4bn to LLC5 on those terms.

The **First-tier Tribunal** disagreed. Judge John Brooks found that an independent lender would have made loans of the same amount, on the same interest terms, provided it received **covenants** (the promises a borrower gives to protect its lender), and that those covenants would have been given.

The **Upper Tribunal** reversed him: you cannot import covenants that never existed in the real deal. Without them the comparison failed, and HMRC won.

The **Court of Appeal** reversed the Upper Tribunal. Falk LJ's reasoning, as the commentaries summarise it: in the real deal the lender belonged to the same group as everyone else in the chain. A stranger lending to LLC5 would face risks the group lender did not, because other group companies might act in ways that damaged the loan. An independent lender would protect itself, so the hypothetical deal must include that protection. The covenants were part of a fair comparison, not an invention, and the FTT's finding was restored. **On transfer pricing, BlackRock won.**

Commentators read one passage of Falk LJ's judgment (para 63 is the one cited) as a hint that HMRC might have done better by looking at the **borrower's** side: would LLC5, if independent, have wanted to borrow at all? That argument was not run and the case did not decide it. Chapter 27 returns to it.

## Why this company borrowed.

**The law says** (CTA 2009 s 441): if a loan relationship has an **unallowable purpose** in an accounting period, the debits are disallowed **so far as attributable** to that purpose **on a just and reasonable apportionment**. A purpose is unallowable if it is not among the company's **business or other commercial purposes** (s 442). A **tax avoidance purpose** counts as commercial only if it is **not the main purpose or one of the main purposes**. The tax advantage need not be the company's own: a tax advantage for **any other person** counts.

The **FTT** found that LLC5 had two main purposes, one commercial and one to obtain a tax advantage, but apportioned all the debits to the commercial purpose. The **UT** treated the commercial benefit as a by-product of a tax-driven decision and apportioned all the debits to the tax purpose.

The **Court of Appeal** agreed with the UT's result, though not with all of its reasoning. It was common ground that purpose is a question of the company's own **subjective intention**. The court began with a plain question: why did LLC5 enter into the loans? The answer was to obtain a tax advantage.

The court did not say that every deductible interest payment is suspect. Falk LJ was careful: awareness that interest is deductible does not make tax a main purpose, and nor does the size of the deduction on its own; something more is needed. Here there was more. LLC5's board did see a commercial margin (dividends in would exceed interest out). But the tax advantage belonged to the group, and the group's plan was why LLC5 was there. Nugee LJ, at [192], repeated Falk LJ's description of taking the loans to obtain that advantage as LLC5's "sole raison d'être".

Then came the **apportionment**. On a "but for" approach, without the tax advantage the loans would not have been made, so **all the debits** were attributable to the unallowable purpose (paras 186–187, 193). None was deductible. The approach echoes *Fidex Ltd v HMRC* [2016] EWCA Civ 385 ("But for this tax avoidance scheme there would have been no debit at all", para 74).

The Supreme Court refused permission to appeal. The Court of Appeal's judgment stands.

> **Status note.** The facts above come from the judgments as summarised on Find Case Law, the Judiciary press summary and practitioner commentaries. The **"sole raison d'être"** words and the paragraph references (97, 186–187, 192–193) were checked against the judgment (9 October 2026). The Supreme Court's permission list prints the date **13 October 2024** (a Sunday) and the citation [2024] EWCA Civ 419; Find Case Law's citation is [2024] EWCA Civ 330, which this book uses.

## Why one loan can get two answers.

The two rules ask different questions, so they can give different answers about the same loan.

| | Transfer pricing (TIOPA 2010 Part 4) | Unallowable purpose (CTA 2009 s 441) |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Are the terms what independent parties would have agreed? | Why did this company enter into the loan relationship? |
| Nature of the test | Objective: a market comparison | Subjective: the company's purposes |
| Ignores | Motive | Whether the rate was fair |
| Effect | Profits computed on arm's length provision (can be no loan at all) | Debits disallowed so far as attributable (just and reasonable) |
| *BlackRock* outcome | Taxpayer won | HMRC won: 100% of debits disallowed |

Transfer pricing is a **valuer's** question; unallowable purpose is a **detective's** question. A loan can pass the market test perfectly and still fail on purpose.

**Misconception: "If an intra-group loan is priced at arm's length, the interest is safe."** Arm's length pricing gets you through the first gate only. *BlackRock* is the proof: the pricing passed, and every pound of the deduction still went.

*BlackRock* was not alone. Within weeks the Court of Appeal decided two more cases on the same rule, both for HMRC: *Kwik-Fit Group Ltd v HMRC* [2024] EWCA Civ 434 (3 May 2024: an intra-group reorganisation of loans so that trapped losses could be used) and *JTI Acquisition Company (2011) Ltd v HMRC* [2024] EWCA Civ 652 (13 June 2024: borrowing to fund a real acquisition, where the tax advantage was "bolted on" to a commercial deal and still everything was disallowed). The Supreme Court refused permission in all three on the same list. Chapter 12 tells the other two stories and the case still on its way up (*Syngenta*).

There is also a gate that BlackRock's 2009 loans never had to pass. The **corporate interest restriction** (TIOPA 2010 Part 10) applies for periods of account starting on or after **1 April 2017**. It caps a worldwide group's net UK interest deductions, under the default fixed ratio method at **30% of aggregate tax-EBITDA** (subject to the debt cap), with a **£2m** de minimis. A group borrowing like this in FY2026 would meet all three gates. Chapter 28 teaches the third.

> **Going further: the three gates for an intra-group loan (FY2026).**
> 1. **Transfer pricing** (TIOPA 2010 Part 4): amount, rate and terms at arm's length? Thin capitalisation is a transfer pricing question. Chapter 27.
> 2. **Unallowable purpose** (CTA 2009 ss 441–442): is a tax advantage, for the company or any other person, a main purpose? If so, how much of the debits is attributable to it on a just and reasonable basis? Chapter 12.
> 3. **Corporate interest restriction** (TIOPA 2010 Part 10): how much net interest can the group deduct in the UK in total? Chapter 28.
>
> Run them in that order in a computation: the transfer pricing and unallowable purpose disallowances come first, and the interest restriction then applies to what is left. (The detailed ordering and the treatment of each disallowance in tax-EBITDA are chapter 28's job.) The tax function's task is to record, at the time, why each group company borrows: purpose is tested subjectively, but tribunals find it from the evidence.

> **Exam lens.**
> - **Grades (2026 grid, v2 extract):** loan relationships (CTA 2009 Part 5, excluding Chapters 7, 10, 11, 13 and 14) **1, core**, so the unallowable purpose rule is core; transfer pricing and advance pricing agreements **1, core** (the row carries the words "Awareness – basic principles only"; chapter 27 deals with what that means); corporate interest restriction **1, core**. Check the 2027 grid when published.
> - **Past appearances:** **M23 Q3 (15 marks)** was a loan from a US company that might take 60% control: transfer pricing (participation condition, thin capitalisation) and CIR, plus withholding. The examiners said the main issues were TP and CIR and that time was wasted on DPT, which does not apply to loan relationships. TP with CIR came again in **M26 Q1** and **N24 Q5**.
> - **Style:** technical prose and computations; "Explain" or "Calculate, with explanations"; 0.5–1 mark per point; no letter format.
> - **Traps:** stopping after the pricing point; raising DPT (the M23 examiners said it does not apply to loan relationships; FA 2026 has since replaced it with the UTPP charge, chapter 30); forgetting that a tax advantage for *another* group company counts under s 441.

## The questions this book asks.

This one loan leads straight into the four questions that run through the book.

1. **Is a group one taxpayer or many?** LLC5 was a separate company with its own return. Yet its purpose was read through the group's plan, and its deficit was used by other companies through group relief.
2. **Where are profits made, and what stops them drifting?** A British link in an American chain created a UK deduction with no matching UK income. Much of this book is about the rules that watch borders.
3. **What does the law follow: the accounts, the deal or its own purpose?** The loan relationship rules start from the accounts; transfer pricing tests the deal against the market; the unallowable purpose rule overrides both when the purpose is wrong.
4. **What must a group's tax function spot?** An adviser who checked only the interest rate would have missed the point that decided the case. The examiner wants you to identify the issues, all of them, and know which specialist rule answers each.

So when you meet an intra-group loan, in practice or in the exam, ask three things. Are the terms what strangers would agree? Why did this company borrow? And how much of the group's interest can the UK take in total? Chapter 27 answers the first, chapter 12 the second and chapter 28 the third.

Most of this book follows an invented group of companies, **Tarnmoor**, whose story begins in chapter 1. Everything about Tarnmoor is made up. BlackRock is real, and so is every rule in this prologue.

Next comes the introduction, and a map of the ground ahead.

# Introduction.

The prologue followed one loan through three courts and found two answers. Keep that picture in mind, because it is a fair picture of the ground ahead. A larger company is not a small company with more noughts on the end. It borrows from its own relatives. It owns companies that own companies. It trades across borders, reports to investors, and answers to a board that must publish its approach to tax. Almost every rule you met in *The Living Law* (TKS) still applies to it. But around those rules sits a second layer of law, written for scale.

This introduction is a map. It sets out the four questions the book keeps asking, the paper the book serves, the way the chapters are arranged, the invented group whose story carries the law, and how the two editions of each chapter work. It ends with some advice on using the book alongside the question practice you already have. The law throughout is the law for **FY2026** (1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027), under **Finance Act 2026** (Royal Assent 18 March 2026).

## Five ways the larger company is different.

**1. Scale.** Size switches rules on. The ladder, for FY2026 (chapter 1 builds it rung by rung):

| Threshold | What it switches on | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| Augmented profits > £1.5m (÷ 1 + associated companies) | Large company: quarterly instalment payments (QIPs), months 7, 10, 13, 16 | 1, 3 |
| Augmented profits > £20m (÷ 1 + associated companies) | Very large company: QIPs in months 3, 6, 9, 12 | 1, 3 |
| Net interest > £2m a year | Corporate interest restriction (CIR) can bite | 28 |
| £5m | Deductions allowance for carried-forward losses (one per group) | 14 |
| UK turnover > £200m or balance sheet > £2bn | Senior accounting officer (SAO), published tax strategy, uncertain tax treatment (UTT) notification | 4 |
| Leaving the SME category | Transfer pricing applies | 27 |
| Consolidated revenue ≥ / > €750m | Country-by-country reporting, TP records (Master File and Local File), Pillar Two | 27, 30 |

**2. The group.** UK law taxes each company separately; there is **no group return** for corporation tax. Yet a group plans, borrows and invests as one business, and the law builds bridges between its companies: group relief for losses, no gain/no loss transfers of assets, group roll-over, a shared AIA and deductions allowance, shared thresholds. Each bridge has its own entry test, and the tests do not match (chapter 1's "guest lists").

**3. The border.** A large group earns profits in many countries and moves money, goods, people and ideas between them. Most of the second half of this book is about the rules that decide where those profits are taxed, and the rules that stop them drifting to wherever tax is lowest.

**4. Governance.** A large company's tax is not only computed. It is managed, certified and reported. HMRC's Large Business directorate says it works with around 2,000 of the largest businesses; its customer compliance managers assess each group's tax risk and how well the group manages it (HMRC's Tax Compliance Risk Management manual, TCRM1000). The law adds personal duties for a named officer (the SAO) and a criminal offence for failing to prevent the facilitation of tax evasion (Criminal Finances Act 2017 ss 45–46).

**5. The accounts.** For a larger company the accounts are not a starting point that tax quickly leaves behind. They decide the timing of loan relationship profits, intangible asset profits and much else (CTA 2009 s 46 and Parts 5, 6 and 8). And the accounts must also show a **tax charge** that investors read, current and deferred, which is a different number from the tax bill (chapter 6).

## Four questions.

Those five differences produce four questions, and the book asks them in every chapter.

1. **One taxpayer or many?** The law taxes each company on its own profits, yet it lets losses travel, assets move and gains be rolled over across the group. Where does it build those bridges, and where does it refuse? Chapters 1, 15 and 17 carry this question furthest, and the CIR (chapter 28) and the global minimum tax (chapter 30) push it in a new direction.
2. **Where are profits made, and what stops them drifting?** Residence, permanent establishments, treaties and the foreign branch exemption decide where profits are taxed. Transfer pricing, controlled foreign companies, hybrid mismatches, the CIR and the global minimum tax stop them moving to where they are not. Part Four is built around this question.
3. **What does the law follow: the accounts, the deal or its own purpose?** Tax starts from the accounts. It respects many commercial transactions, such as share exchanges and demergers, on their own terms. And then, again and again, it asks why a company did something, and overrides both the accounts and the deal when the answer is tax. The prologue's loan was the first example. It will not be the last.
4. **How does a large group govern its tax, and what must an adviser spot?** The CIOT says candidates for this paper "are not expected to have deep knowledge of all tax areas but should be able to identify what the potential tax issues are". So every chapter asks what the tax function must do, by when, and what a good adviser would flag.

## The paper this book serves.

This book is written for the **CTA Advanced Technical paper, Taxation of Larger Companies and Groups** (LCG). Until 2023 it was called Taxation of Major Corporates.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Duration | 3 hours 30 minutes |
| Shape | Normally 6 questions of 10, 15 or 20 marks; 100 marks; usually three 20s, two 15s and one 10 |
| Pass mark | 50% |
| Scenarios | "Typically be based around multinational groups and larger companies that may be listed, with no individual controlling shareholders" |
| Syllabus elements | (1) CT including CT on chargeable gains; (2) capital allowances; (3) stamp duty and SDLT at awareness level |
| Core rule | At least 70% of the CT element from core material |
| Grades (syllabus grid) | 1 = core (depth, computations); 2 = non-core (working knowledge, main computation); 3 = awareness (recognise and state) |
| Likely sitting | **4 May 2027, 2.30pm** (fallback **26 October 2027, 2.30pm**) |
| Law for 2027 sittings | FA 2026 (the settled pattern: year N exams test the Finance Act of year N–1) |
| Style | Technical prose and computations; no letter, report or email format |

So owner-managed companies, close company loans and profit extraction are not this paper's business, and they are not this book's either.

The grid this book follows is the **2026 grid**. As this book was finished, in October 2026, the CIOT had not yet published a grid, a prospectus or tax tables for 2027. When they appear, check them against what this book says (each reading edition's Exam lens gives the 2026 grade).

The book also follows the paper's habits. Across the seven sittings from May 2023 to May 2026:

| Topic | Appearances M23–M26 | Main chapters |
|---|---|---|
| CT computation (15–20 marks) | Every sitting | 7 (with 3, 6, 8, 14) |
| Capital allowances | Nearly every paper, standalone or embedded | 8, 9 |
| Groups and consortia | 6 | 15 |
| Property gains, leases, group roll-over | 5 | 16, 17 |
| SSE, shares and reorganisations | 5 | 18 |
| International (residence, PE, branch exemption, migration) | Every sitting since N24 | 22–25 |
| Controlled foreign companies | 4 (two full 20-mark questions) | 26 |
| Transfer pricing | 5 | 27 |
| Corporate interest restriction | 4 | 28 |
| Compliance and governance | 8 | 3, 4 |

The longest chapters in this book sit where the marks have been. Chapter 32 gives the rest of the evidence: the examiners' recurring messages, the layouts and the timing.

## How the book is built.

After this introduction come 32 chapters in five Parts, then a conclusion and a note on sources.

| Part | Chapters | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| **One: The Larger Company** | 1–4 | What makes a company large and who counts as its group; where corporate tax law lives; returns, payments and enquiries; governance and the anti-avoidance architecture |
| **Two: Measuring Profit** | 5–14 | Tax follows the accounts; deferred tax; the large company computation; plant and machinery; buildings, fixtures, leasing and successions; R&D; intangibles and IP; loan relationships and derivatives; companies with investment business; losses |
| **Three: The Group** | 15–21 | Group relief, consortia and JVs; company gains on property and leases; gains inside the group; shares, the SSE, reorganisations and earn-outs; reconstructions, demergers and distributions; buying and selling companies; stamp taxes for groups |
| **Four: Across Borders** | 22–30 | Residence and migration; non-resident companies, PEs and withholding; treaties and DTR; branch or subsidiary; CFCs; transfer pricing and APAs; the CIR; hybrid mismatches; the global minimum and the end of DPT |
| **Five: Putting It Together** | 31–32 | The Ridgeway deal (one acquisition through every relevant rule, as a long exam question does); the Advanced Technical craft (software, resources, timing, layouts, examiner messages) |

## Where *The Living Law* ends.

This book assumes that you know *The Living Law*, the earlier book written for the Tax Knowledge and Skills paper. It does not teach those foundations twice. Where a chapter builds on one, it recaps it in one to three sentences and names the chapter ("*The Living Law*, chapter 24, on groups"). Then it goes further.

Going further means two things:

- **Taught again, in full, at Advanced Technical depth:** topics *The Living Law* touched, such as group relief, loan relationships, R&D, company gains and the foreign branch exemption, because the AT examiner expects mastery, not recall.
- **Taught from first principles:** topics *The Living Law* only signposted: transfer pricing, CFCs, the CIR, hybrid mismatches, the global minimum tax, company migration, deferred tax and demergers.

## Tarnmoor, an invented group.

Most chapters follow one group of companies, **Tarnmoor**. **Everything about Tarnmoor is invented for teaching**: its companies, people, numbers and its two overseas countries, **Vallaria** and **Marrovia**. Ireland is real, and so are its 12.5% trading rate and its treaty with the UK (as modified by the MLI), but Tarnmoor's Irish company is not.

**Tarnmoor plc** is a listed engineering group with its head office in Leeds and no controlling shareholder. It was built to match the examiner's description of a typical scenario, and to be large enough to switch on every regime the paper tests (GY1 consolidated revenue £1,180m). Its main trading company, Tarnmoor Engineering, makes industrial valves, actuators and pumps. Around it sit a property company, a treasury company, a joint venture (Helmside), overseas subsidiaries in Vallaria, Marrovia and Ireland, and the companies it buys and sells as the story runs.

The story begins in chapter 1, when Tarnmoor buys **Calder Valve Engineering** for **£32m**. If you have read *The Living Law*, you know Calder: the invented valve maker where **Dan Hartley** worked as an engineer, and his story continues here. So does his sister **Jess**'s. Some years after the rest of the group's story, Tarnmoor buys her business, Ridgeway, and chapter 31 tells that deal.

**Group Years.** Tarnmoor lives in Group Years (GY1, GY2, ...), not calendar years. Group Years are Tarnmoor's accounting years to 31 December; GY1 is the year in which Calder joins. No calendar year is ever attached to a Tarnmoor event, and **every Tarnmoor computation applies FY2026 law**, whichever Group Year the story has reached. Real rules start on real dates (for example, "accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026"). Where a chapter needs to teach a real commencement date, it uses a **labelled example with real dates**, outside the story. That keeps the story simple and the dates honest.

The story is the spine of the book, not its cage. When the examiner tests a variation the story never reaches, a chapter says "suppose" and works a labelled example. Those examples never become part of the story.

## Two editions.

Every chapter comes in two editions.

**The audio script** is written to be heard once. Numbers are spoken as words, and worked examples are told as stories with a few memorable figures. Each script ends with **"What to take away"**, a spoken recap. The spoken conventions:

| Written (reading edition) | Spoken (audio script) |
|---|---|
| CTA 2009 / CTA 2010 | "the two thousand and nine Act" / "the twenty ten Act" (full name first in each chapter) |
| TIOPA 2010 | "the Taxation, International and Other Provisions, Act twenty ten", then "the International Act" |
| TCGA 1992 | "the Gains Act" |
| CAA 2001 / TMA 1970 | "the Capital Allowances Act" / "the Management Act" |
| CTA 2010 s 1141 | "section eleven forty one" (four-digit sections in pairs) |
| TCGA 1992 s 171; CTA 2009 s 441 | "section one seven one"; "section four four one" (practitioners' digit-by-digit names) |
| HMRC; CFC | "H M R C"; "controlled foreign company", then "C F C" (spaced letters, declared first) |
| GAAR; DOTAS; GloBE | Spoken as words |
| £1.35m; 14.99%; €750m | "one point three five million pounds"; "fourteen point nine nine per cent"; "seven hundred and fifty million euros" |

**The reading edition** is the same chapter for the page: digits, statutory references ("s 441 CTA 2009"; "TIOPA 2010 s 371BC"), standard case citations (*BlackRock HoldCo 5, LLC v HMRC* [2024] EWCA Civ 330), and every computation laid out as the examiner expects, with **£ or £000, never both, in each table**. It adds three kinds of box:

- **Worked example**: the full numbers behind each story, and labelled extra examples.
- **Going further**: planning, the tax function's tasks and deadlines, interaction between regimes, judgement and ethics.
- **Exam lens**: each topic's grade on the 2026 grid, its past appearances (sitting, question, marks), what the examiners said, the style, the traps and the layout.

Each reading edition ends with a **Key rules and figures** table and a **Statutory and case references** list.

**Status words** are the same in both editions:

| Words | Meaning |
|---|---|
| "The law says" | Statute |
| "The courts have held" | Case law |
| "HMRC's view is" | Guidance: not law |
| "Disputed" / "being litigated" | Not settled |
| "Announced" | A government statement |
| "Proposed, not law" | A consultation or draft legislation Parliament has not passed |
| "In our invented case" | Tarnmoor and the Hartleys |

## How to use this book.

The book teaches. It does not test. There are no practice questions here, because you have the CIOT's past papers and your own question bank, and those are the right tools for practice.

A good rhythm:

1. **Listen** to a chapter for the story and the reasons.
2. **Read** its reading edition with a pen, working each computation yourself.
3. **Sit a past question** on the same topic, under time (about 2.1 minutes a mark), and mark it against the CIOT's suggested answer and marking guide.
4. **Read the examiners' report** for that sitting, and, from May 2024, the **banded example scripts**. Comparing a scraped pass with a strong answer to the same question is one of the best lessons available; chapter 32 shows what to look for.

Practise on the student legislation product you will use on the day, **Croner-i or Tolley**, because in the exam the legislation is your only reference. And practise with the right numbers:

| Item | 2026 tax tables (FA 2025) | Law for a 2027 sitting (FA 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Main pool WDA | 18% | **14%** (chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026; hybrid rate for straddling periods) |
| 40% FYA (new main-rate plant) | — | **Available** (expenditure from 1 January 2026) |
| Special rate WDA | 6% | 6% |

When the 2027 tables appear, check every rate against them.

Finally, keep the status words in your ear. Several things described in this book are **proposals, not law**. A draft Finance Bill 2026-27 was published on **13 July 2026**, and a Budget is due on **28 October 2026**. None of that changes the law for your sitting. The conclusion says what may be coming, and the note on sources says how to keep up.

So the book starts where Tarnmoor's story starts, on 1 April in GY1, with a family firm that becomes one company among many.

# Part One: The Larger Company

## Chapter 1: One company or many?

On 1 April, at the start of what our story will call Group Year One (GY1), a regional engineering business owned by one family stopped being a family firm. Calder Valve Engineering Ltd woke up that morning as it had gone to bed: same works, same 300 staff, same order book. By lunchtime its shares belonged to Tarnmoor plc, an invented listed engineering group, which had paid £32m for them.

Readers of *The Living Law* (TKS) have met Calder before. It is invented too, like every company and person in Tarnmoor's story. In *The Living Law*, chapter 5, Calder was a company on its own with no associated companies: taxable total profits (TTP) of £2,000,000 and corporation tax of £500,000, paid in four quarterly instalments of £125,000. One company, one return, one bill.

Nothing in the purchase changed Calder's legal identity. It still computes its own profits, files its own return and owes its own tax. And yet, from that 1 April, almost every number around it moves. The point at which it must pay tax early moves. The rules on how it prices its dealings with sister companies switch on. A board in Leeds now answers for its tax governance. Its interest costs are tested against a group it has never met.

So here is the question this chapter answers. **When a company joins a large group, is it still one taxpayer among many, or has it become a small part of one large taxpayer?** The short answer is both, and the skill of this paper lies in knowing which rule takes which view.

This is the first chapter of Part One, on the larger company. It sets up the whole book and builds on *The Living Law*, chapter 20 (corporation tax foundations) and chapter 24 (groups). No single syllabus row belongs to it. Instead it gives you two tools used in every later chapter, a **threshold ladder** and a **group-definitions matrix**, and introduces the invented group whose story runs through the book.

---

## Meet Tarnmoor

Tarnmoor plc is our invented parent company: incorporated in England, head office in Leeds, shares listed on the main market of the London Stock Exchange. Nobody controls it; its shareholders are pension funds, insurers and thousands of private investors. That shape is deliberate. The CIOT describes the paper's scenarios this way: "Scenarios will typically be based around multinational groups and larger companies that may be listed, with no individual controlling shareholders." Tarnmoor is exactly that kind of group.

**The Tarnmoor group at 1 April GY1 (all invented except Ireland)**

| Company (short form) | Incorporated / resident | Ownership | Year end | Role |

| Tarnmoor plc (TPLC) | England / UK | Listed, widely held | 31 Dec | Ultimate parent; company with investment business |
| Tarnmoor Engineering Ltd (TEL) | England / UK | TPLC 100% | 31 Dec | Main trading company (valves, actuators, pumps); GY1 revenue £630m |
| Tarnmoor Estates Ltd (TES) | England / UK | TPLC 100% | 31 Dec | Group property company |
| Tarnmoor Finance Ltd (TFL) | England / UK | TPLC 100% | 31 Dec | Treasury; £550m 5.5% listed notes |
| Tarnmoor Water Systems Ltd (TWS) | England / UK | TPLC 100% | 31 Dec | Water-infrastructure trade |
| Calder Valve Engineering Ltd (CVE) | England / UK | TPLC 100% from 1 April GY1 (Oldroyd family before) | 31 Mar | Acquired for £32m |
| Tarnmoor Pumps Ltd | England / UK | TPLC 100% | — | Dormant throughout |
| Tarnmoor Vallaria SA (TVS) | Vallaria / Vallaria (invented country) | TPLC 100% | 31 Dec | Overseas manufacturer and distributor |

Group Years are Tarnmoor's accounting years to 31 December. We never attach a calendar year to them, and **every computation applies the law for FY2026** (1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027) under Finance Act 2026, whatever Group Year the story has reached.

In GY1 consolidated revenue is **£1,180m** (TEL £630m; TVS £330m; TWS £110m; Calder £48m for nine months, about £64m a year; TIL £60m; TES third-party rents £2m), and the group employs about 6,000 people. Three invented people will guide us: **Nadia Kerr**, Tarnmoor's CFO; **Tom Hesketh**, group head of tax; and **Graham Pike**, Calder's finance director before and after the deal.

And **Dan Hartley**, the chartered engineer from *The Living Law*, works in Calder's process valves division. Readers of TKS chapters 8 to 10 followed his commute, his benefits and his pay; by now his long secondment to a client's plant on Teesside is over. They also know how his time at Calder ends. This book shows the company's side of that story. For now, Dan is about to be asked to give most of his time to a new research project (chapter 10).

---

## Why one company stays one taxpayer

*The Living Law*, chapter 20, told how a company became a person in law. The leading case is *Salomon v A Salomon and Co Ltd* [1897] AC 22 (HL): a properly formed company is a legal person distinct from its members, however its shares are held. Corporation tax, created by the Finance Act 1965, was built on that foundation. The taxpayer is the company.

This is the **separate entity principle**. Each company in a group computes its own TTP for its own accounting periods, on its own CT600, and pays its own tax. Each has its own losses, capital allowance pools and base costs. If TES sells a building to TEL, two taxpayers have dealt with each other.

Why does the law insist on this when a group plainly runs as one business?

- **Company law** gives each company its own assets and debts; its creditors look only to it.
- **Groups change shape** constantly. A system based on the separate company follows acquisitions and disposals without reopening a consolidated position.
- **Minority shareholders** (Greyfell and Northlight in Helmside) need each company's profit to be its own.
- **A buyer inherits the company's tax history**, which only makes sense if that history belongs to the company.

But the principle has costs: a loss in one company and a profit in a sister would be taxed as if strangers held them, and an asset moved between sisters would trigger a gain though nothing has left the group. So Parliament has built a **toolkit of bridges**: group and consortium relief (CTA 2010 Parts 5 and 5A), no gain, no loss transfers within a gains group (TCGA 1992 s 171), group roll-over (s 175), group relief from stamp duty (FA 1930 s 42) and SDLT (FA 2003 Sch 7).

The UK never abandons the separate entity; it bridges it, rule by rule, each bridge with its own conditions. Only in its newest regimes, the **corporate interest restriction** (TIOPA 2010 Part 10) and **Pillar Two** (F(No.2)A 2023 Parts 3–4), does the law begin to treat the group as a single economic unit. That tension is the book's first debate (L1), developed in chapters 15, 28 and 30.

---

## The group's tax charge is not its tax bill

> **Misconception.** *The Living Law*, chapter 24, tackled "a group pays tax as one". The grown-up version is: **"the tax charge in the consolidated accounts is the group's tax bill."**

People believe it because it is the number they see. Tarnmoor's annual report shows one income tax expense, and analysts quote the effective tax rate that comes from it.

But the consolidated charge is an accounting figure:

- it adds current tax across **every** company, UK and overseas, so it includes Vallarian and Marrovian tax that HMRC never sees;
- it includes **deferred tax**, which is not a payment but a recognition of tax that will fall due, or be saved, in later years (chapter 6);
- it reflects consolidation adjustments that no tax return contains.

The UK tax bill is a set of **separate liabilities, company by company**, each computed on that company's TTP and paid on its own timetable. In GY1, TEL's CT after group and consortium relief is **£2,633,750** (TTP £10.535m × 25%); Calder, in its first group accounting period, computes CT of **£750,000** (TTP £3.0m × 25%) before setting off its RDEC. There is **no group return** for corporation tax.

There is a second reason the two numbers differ. The accounts measure profit under accounting standards; tax law then adjusts it, adding back some costs, deducting others, replacing depreciation with capital allowances. Some differences reverse later and some never do. The consolidated charge captures the reversing ones as deferred tax; the return simply taxes this year's adjusted profit.

The practical lesson is that a tax function **reconciles**: it explains the consolidated charge to the board, auditors and market, builds up the company returns underneath it, and makes the two stories agree. "The tax charge in the accounts" and "the tax payable" are different requirements with different answers, and tax-accounting tails to computation questions are now common (N25 Q1, M25 Q2, M24 Q2; a standalone 10-mark deferred tax question in M26 Q6).

---

## House rules with their own guest lists

*The Living Law*, chapter 24, pictured a group as a family of separate wallets living under one roof, with house rules about when money can pass between them. The extension this book needs: **each house rule has its own guest list.** Who counts as family depends on which rule you are applying.

The matrix below is owned by this chapter and applied throughout the book. Learn it as a matrix: the exam rarely names the test; it describes a shareholding and expects you to see which lists it puts a company on.

**Group-definitions matrix (FY2026)**

| Guest list | Test | Who counts | Used for | Authority | Chapter |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Associated companies** | Control (one controls the other, or both under common control; CTA 2010 ss 450–451 meaning) | Any company, **UK or overseas**; a company carrying on no trade or business (e.g. dormant) is ignored; a **passive holding company** is treated as carrying on no business | Marginal relief limits (£50,000 / £250,000 divided by 1 + associates); QIP thresholds (HMRC guidance: divided by associated companies, replacing related 51% group companies, from 2023) | CTA 2010 Part 3A, ss 18E–18F; SI 1998/3175 reg 3; CTM92520, CTM92800 | 3, 7 |
| **51% group** | > 50% of ordinary share capital, directly or indirectly | Parent and its 51% subsidiaries (any residence) | Group payment arrangements; SSE group (and aggregation for the 10% test); recovery of unpaid CT on gains; tax strategy and UTT group size tests | CTA 2010 s 1154; TMA 1970 s 59F; TCGA 1992 Sch 7AC para 26, s 190(13); FA 2016 Sch 19; FA 2022 Sch 17 | 3, 4, 17, 18 |
| **75% group (group relief)** | ≥ 75% of ordinary share capital **and** ≥ 75% of profits available for distribution and of assets on a winding up (equity holder tests) | Losses pass only between **UK related** companies (UK resident, or non-resident with a UK permanent establishment) | Group relief (Part 5); carried-forward group relief (Part 5A) | CTA 2010 ss 151(4), 152 ff (Ch 6) | 15 |
| **Consortium** | ≥ 75% of a trading or holding company's ordinary share capital owned by companies each holding ≥ 5% | Members and the consortium company; link companies | Consortium relief, limited by the member's ownership proportion | CTA 2010 ss 132–133, 143, 153 | 15 |
| **Gains group** | Principal company + its 75% subsidiaries (and theirs), each an **effective 51% subsidiary** of the principal (profits and assets) | Overseas companies can be members; a company is in only one gains group | No gain, no loss transfers; s 171A reallocation; group roll-over; pre-entry losses; degrouping | TCGA 1992 s 170 | 17 |
| **Stamp duty group** | Parent holds ≥ 75% of ordinary share capital, profits and assets | Bodies corporate | Stamp duty group relief, denied where arrangements exist for a person to obtain control of the transferee but not the transferor | FA 1930 s 42 | 21 |
| **SDLT group** | 75% of ordinary share capital, profits and assets | Companies | SDLT group relief; denied for arrangements for the purchaser to leave the group (and other conditions); 3-year clawback | FA 2003 Sch 7 paras 1–3 | 21 |
| **Worldwide group** | Ultimate parent + subsidiaries consolidated under international accounting standards | All consolidated entities, any residence, including dormant subsidiaries | Corporate interest restriction | TIOPA 2010 ss 373, 473–474 (Part 10 Ch 11); CFM95330 | 28 |
| **MNE group (Pillar Two)** | Consolidated group | All consolidated members | MTT/DTT; €750m threshold | F(No.2)A 2023 s 129 | 30 |
| **CbC group** | Consolidated group | All consolidated members | Country-by-country reporting; TP records | SI 2016/237 reg 3; SI 2023/818 | 27 |
| **TP participation** | One party directly or indirectly participates in the management, control or capital of the other (or common participation) | Any persons | Transfer pricing (Part 4) | TIOPA 2010 s 148 | 27 |
| **CFC control** | Legal or economic control (> 50% of proceeds, income or assets on a winding up); accounting control (with a 50% condition); the 40% joint-venture rule | Non-UK resident companies controlled from the UK | CFC charge (with a separate 25% interest test for apportionment) | TIOPA 2010 ss 371RB–371RE | 26 |
| **"Group other than a small group"** | Companies Act 2006 small group tests | Members of medium and large groups | Enquiry window runs from the filing date | FA 1998 Sch 18 para 24 | 3 |

## Applying the guest lists to Tarnmoor

Run Tarnmoor through the lists in GY1 and the family changes shape.

**Associated companies.** TPLC controls everything it owns outright: TPLC, TEL, TES, TFL, TWS, TVS, TCM, TIL, and Calder from 1 April. **Nine.** The two overseas companies count (association turns on control, not residence). Tarnmoor Pumps does not count (dormant). Helmside does not count: 45% is not control, and no single shareholder controls it. For marginal relief a company counts if associated **at any time in the AP**, so each company's limits are divided by **9** at once (itself plus eight associates). The QIP count is taken on a different day (see "Tarnmoor on the ladder").

**Group relief.** Every wholly owned company passes the 75% tests, but losses pass only between UK related companies. TVS and TCM are outside the charge, so their losses stay abroad. **TIL**, though incorporated in Ireland, is UK resident while its board meets in Leeds, so it can surrender and claim like any other UK company. **Helmside** is not in the group relief group at all: it is a **consortium company**, and its losses flow in proportion to the members' holdings (chapter 15).

**Gains group.** Almost the same list, overseas companies included, with TPLC as principal company.

**Worldwide group (CIR).** TPLC and every subsidiary in its consolidated accounts, including TVS, TCM and the dormant Pumps company. Helmside sits outside it as an unconsolidated joint venture.

| Company | Associated (marginal relief divisor 9) | 75% group relief group | Gains group | Worldwide group | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TPLC | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ (principal) | ✓ (ultimate parent) | |
| TEL, TES, TFL, TWS | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Calder (from 1 April GY1) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Joins every list at once |
| TIL | ✓ | ✓ (UK resident) | ✓ | ✓ | Irish-incorporated |
| TVS, TCM | ✓ | ✗ (not UK related) | ✓ | ✓ | Overseas |
| Tarnmoor Pumps | ✗ (dormant) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | Nothing to surrender |
| Helmside | ✗ (45%) | ✗ (consortium) | ✗ | ✗ | Consortium company |

So which is the real Tarnmoor group? There is no single answer, and that is the lesson. Move a building from TES to TEL, and the gains group and the SDLT group matter. Lend from TFL to TVS, and the transfer pricing participation test matters. Borrow from a bank, and the worldwide group matters.

Calder's purchase shows why. On 1 April it joins every list at once, and each membership switches on a different consequence. The rest of this chapter is about the consequences that come from size.

---

## What makes a company larger: the threshold ladder

The paper's title speaks of larger companies; this book uses **"larger company"** as a working term, not a legal one. No statute defines it. Instead, dozens of rules each draw their own line.

Why should size matter? Three reasons recur:

1. **Revenue.** A small number of large businesses pay a large share of corporation tax, so the state wants their money sooner and their risks visible.
2. **Capability.** A group with a tax function, auditors and systems can carry burdens that would crush a small company.
3. **International consensus.** Working through the OECD, governments have agreed common lines, most famously **€750m** of revenue, above which country-by-country reporting and the global minimum tax apply.

Every line is a **cliff edge**: one pound or euro either side changes a company's obligations, and groups cross thresholds by accident through acquisitions, mergers, currency movements or one good year.

**The threshold ladder (FY2026)** — owned by this chapter and reused throughout the book

| Rung | Measure | Threshold | What it switches on | Authority | Status | Chapter |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marginal relief | Augmented profits | Lower limit £50,000, upper limit £250,000, each divided by 1 + associated companies (associated at any time in the AP) and time-apportioned | Small profits rate 19% / marginal relief (fraction 3/200) below the upper limit; main rate 25% above | CTA 2010 Part 3A | V | 7 |
| Large company (QIPs) | Augmented profits | > **£1.5m**, divided by 1 + associated companies counted on the day before the AP begins, reduced for short periods | Instalments in months 7, 10, 13 and 16; first-year exception where not large in the previous 12 months and profits ≤ £10m (divided) | SI 1998/3175 reg 3; CTM92520, CTM92530 | V (rates) / guidance (divisor) | 3 |
| Very large company (QIPs) | Augmented profits | > **£20m**, divided by 1 + associated companies counted on the day before the AP begins, reduced for short periods | Instalments in months 3, 6, 9 and 12; **no** first-year exception | SI 1998/3175 (APs beginning on or after 1 April 2019); CTM92800, CTM92530 | V / guidance (divisor) | 3 |
| CIR de minimis | Worldwide group's aggregate net tax-interest expense | > **£2m** a year (pro rata for long or short periods) | Interest restriction can bite; below it no restriction | TIOPA 2010 s 392(3) | V | 28 |
| Deductions allowance | Profits against which carried-forward losses are set | **£5m** per company or group per 12 months | Only 50% of profits above the allowance can be relieved by carried-forward losses; one allowance per group (nomination needed) | CTA 2010 Part 7ZA (ss 269ZR–269ZV) | V | 14 |
| UTT notification | Tax advantage | > **£5m** | Notify uncertain tax treatments (if also above the £200m/£2bn rung) | FA 2022 Sch 17 | V | 4 |
| SAO | Turnover / balance sheet of UK-incorporated companies, aggregated across UK group companies, **preceding** financial year | > **£200m** turnover and/or > **£2bn** balance sheet total | Senior accounting officer main duty and annual certificate; company notification | FA 2009 Sch 46 | V | 4 |
| Tax strategy | Turnover / balance sheet of UK group (51% test), previous financial year | > **£200m** and/or > **£2bn** (or a UK member of a €750m CbC group) | Publish a board-approved tax strategy | FA 2016 Sch 19 | V (GOV.UK guidance) | 4 |
| UTT | UK turnover / balance sheet of the 51% group's CT-paying members, previous financial year | > **£200m** and/or > **£2bn** | UTT notifications | FA 2022 Sch 17 paras 2–5 | V | 4 |
| International movements of capital | Value of reportable event | > **£100m** | Report to HMRC within 6 months | FA 2009 Sch 17 | V | 25 |
| CbC reporting | Consolidated group revenue | **€750m** | Country-by-country report | SI 2016/237 reg 3 | V (threshold) | 27 |
| TP records | As CbC | **€750m** | UK members keep and preserve a Master File and Local File (APs beginning on or after 1 April 2023) | SI 2023/818 | V | 27 |
| Pillar Two | Consolidated revenue | "Exceeds" **€750m** in at least 2 of the previous 4 accounting periods (HMRC guidance says "€750m or more") | Multinational and domestic top-up tax; registration and GloBE return | F(No.2)A 2023 s 129 | V (wording discrepancy) | 30 |
| TP SME exemption (the line that runs the other way) | Staff, turnover, balance sheet of the enterprise with linked and partner enterprises | Medium: < 250 staff and turnover ≤ €50m or balance sheet ≤ €43m | Below it, most transfer pricing does not apply (subject to exceptions); above it, TP applies | TIOPA 2010 ss 166, 172; Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC; INTM412080 | V (statute) / S (thresholds) | 27 |
| Advance tax clearances (new) | Expected UK expenditure on a qualifying investment project | ≥ **£1bn** | Binding clearance for 5 years | FA 2026 ss 266–274 | V | 2 |

Two further points. HMRC's Large Business directorate works with most UK businesses whose turnover exceeds £200m (GOV.UK, "HMRC's compliance approach for large businesses"). And the thresholds use **different numbers, from different accounts, over different periods**: profits of the current accounting period (QIPs), the previous financial year (SAO, tax strategy, UTT), two of the previous four periods (Pillar Two). Applying one test to all of them is a classic error.

> **Exam lens: thresholds and groups**
> - **Grades (2026 grid):** CT self-assessment 1; SAO 1; tax strategy 1; group relief (consortia included for LCG) 1; CIR 1; TP and APAs 1; CFCs 1; notification of uncertain tax treatment 3; MTT and DTT 3. No row is "thresholds": they are tested inside these rows.
> - **Past appearances:** **N24 Q5 (20 marks)**: a US multinational buys a UK SME; the marking guide gave 4 marks for filing and QIPs in a large group (thresholds divided across the group, payment dates), 3 for CbC reporting, 6.5 for TP now applying (not an SME) with master and local file contents, 3.5 for CIR (file to protect the position, reporting company, abbreviated return) and 3 for stamp duty on the share purchase. Examiners: most found TP, but some wrote at length on it and ignored easier points; some raised hybrids with no trigger. **N23 Q5 (10 marks)**: SAO thresholds known but misapplied (which companies count). **M25 Q3 (15 marks)**: tax strategy thresholds with different year ends; candidates apportioned subsidiaries' figures instead of using the accounts for the year ending in the parent's financial year. **M25 Q2**: very large company instalments with changing forecasts done badly.
> - **Style:** technical prose; list the obligations a transaction switches on, with the threshold and the authority; 0.5–1 mark per point.
> - **Traps:** dividing by the wrong number (associated companies, counting the company itself), or counting on the wrong day (QIPs: the day before the AP begins; marginal relief: any time in the AP); forgetting that overseas companies count as associates; SAO applies to **UK-incorporated** companies; very large companies have no first-year exception; mixing the tests' measurement periods; treating TP as optional once a target joins a large group.
> - **Layout:** a short table or numbered list of obligations, each with threshold, deadline and penalty.

## Tarnmoor on the ladder

> **Worked example: Tarnmoor and Calder in GY1 (invented figures; FY2026 law)**
>
> **Group-level rungs**
>
> | Test | Tarnmoor GY1 | Threshold | Result |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Consolidated revenue (£m) | 1,180 | — | — |
> | at the story's assumed €1.15 per £ (€m) | 1,357 | €750m | Above: CbC report; TP Master/Local File; Pillar Two (the story assumes revenue has been above €750m for years) |
> | UK turnover (TEL alone, £m) | 630 | £200m | Above: SAO, tax strategy, UTT |
> | Aggregate net tax-interest expense (£m) | 24.65 | £2m | Above: CIR applies (GY1 disallowance £2.21m, chapter 28) |
>
> The €1.15 rate is invented for illustration only; even at parity revenue would exceed €750m.
>
> **Thresholds for each 31 December Tarnmoor company in GY1: two counts**
>
> Marginal relief counts a company associated **at any time** in the AP, so Calder counts at once: divisor **9**. HMRC's manuals (CTM92530; COM95001) count associates for QIPs **on the day before the AP begins**: on 31 December before GY1 the association was TPLC, TEL, TES, TFL, TWS, TVS, TCM and TIL, so the QIP divisor is **8**.
>
> | | £ |
> |---|---|
> | Marginal relief lower limit: £50,000 ÷ 9 | 5,556 |
> | Marginal relief upper limit: £250,000 ÷ 9 | 27,778 |
> | QIP large: £1,500,000 ÷ 8 | 187,500 |
> | QIP very large: £20,000,000 ÷ 8 | 2,500,000 |
>
> **Calder before and after**
>
> | | Calder alone (TKS ch 5) | Calder's first group AP (1 April GY1 – 31 March GY2) |
> |---|---|---|
> | Associated companies | 0 (divisor 1) | For QIPs (counted 31 March GY1, the day before the AP): 0 (divisor 1); for marginal relief (any time in the AP): 8 (divisor 9) |
> | TTP (£) | 2,000,000 | 3,000,000 |
> | Large threshold (£) | 1,500,000 | 1,500,000 |
> | Very large threshold (£) | 20,000,000 | 20,000,000 |
> | Status | Large (was large in the prior period) | **Large** (large before, so no first-year exception) |
> | CT at 25% (£) | 500,000 | 750,000 (before RDEC set-off of £400,000: £350,000 payable) |
> | Instalments | Months 7, 10, 13, 16: 4 × £125,000 | Months 7, 10, 13, 16: 4 × £187,500 (14 October GY1; 14 January, 14 April, 14 July GY2); the RDEC does not reduce them (CIRD89870; chapter 3) |
>
> Calder's TTP rose from £2.0m to £3.0m, still far below the stand-alone £20m line. On 31 March GY2, the day before its next AP, it has eight associates: QIP divisor 9, very large threshold £20,000,000 ÷ 9 = £2,222,222. So Calder becomes **very large one period later**, paying in months 3, 6, 9 and 12 from its AP beginning 1 April GY2: its payment timetable moves four months earlier because it acquired eight associates.
>
> **Transfer pricing.** With about 300 staff, Calder was never a small or medium-sized enterprise (fewer than 250 staff is required). Many targets are; when they join a group like Tarnmoor the SME exemption is lost, because the size test includes linked enterprises. Calder's dealings with TVS will be priced at arm's length, and tested (chapter 27).
>
> **SAO.** Nadia Kerr is SAO for every UK-incorporated group company. TIL is UK resident but **incorporated in Ireland**, so it is outside the SAO rules, which apply to UK-incorporated companies. (How the "preceding financial year" test applies to a company joining part-way through a year is taken up in chapter 4.)

---

## Who does the work

A larger company's tax is done by a system, and the paper expects you to know the parts.

- **The group tax function** (Tom Hesketh's team in our invented case): prepares or reviews every company's return; manages instalments; runs TP documentation; prepares the CIR return and the tax numbers in the accounts; keeps the threshold and group-list map.
- **The board**: approves the published tax strategy; owns the group's tax risk appetite.
- **The CFO as senior accounting officer** (Nadia Kerr): takes reasonable steps to ensure appropriate tax accounting arrangements and certifies each year (FA 2009 Sch 46).
- **The audit committee and external auditors**: test the tax numbers in the accounts.
- **HMRC**: the Large Business directorate works with around 2,000 of the UK's largest businesses; each has a **Customer Compliance Manager** who learns the business and coordinates HMRC's specialists. HMRC's Tax Compliance Risk Management manual (TCRM1000) describes rating customers' tax risk on a spectrum from low to high. A good relationship means issues raised early and resolved in real time.
- **Specialists**: TP economists, valuers, R&D claim teams, stamp taxes lawyers, IFRS specialists.

The work runs to a calendar: instalments through the year; year-end tax numbers for the annual report; returns within 12 months, with the CIR return; the SAO certificate by the end of the accounts filing period (6 months after the year end for a public company, 9 months otherwise). Each deadline belongs to a particular company, and each miss carries its own penalty (chapters 3 and 4).

The CIOT's description of the paper explains why this matters. Candidates "are not expected to have deep knowledge of all tax areas but should be able to identify what the potential tax issues are", and should know specialist areas well enough to "coordinate the work of the firm's specialists". Read that as a job description: the examiner rewards the adviser who sees every issue a transaction raises, says precisely what it means, and knows who to call.

---

## Mapping the thresholds every year

> **Going further: the tax function's threshold map**
>
> A tax function maps every threshold and every group list **every year**, and again whenever the group changes shape.
>
> - **Acquisitions** are the usual trigger. A group just under €750m can cross it by buying one company; CbC reporting, TP records and Pillar Two follow.
> - **Each new subsidiary changes the associated company count**, lowering every company's thresholds. When Tarnmoor buys Brackenwell Sensors Ltd (invented) on 1 July GY2, the marginal relief count rises to 10 at once; the QIP thresholds fall to £2,000,000 / £150,000 (£20m and £1.5m ÷ 10) from GY3.
> - **Disposals and demergers** work the other way (the marginal relief count is 11 in GY5 and GY6 and 10 in GY7; the QIP count stays at 10).
> - **Currency**: the highest line is drawn in euros, so a weaker pound can carry a sterling group across it without a single extra sale.
>
> **A joiner's checklist** (picked up in chapters 3, 4, 10, 14 and 20): different year end (Calder keeps 31 March until GY3); returns and instalments to take over, on an earlier timetable once the QIP count catches up (for Calder, one period later); losses restricted after a change in ownership; loss of SME status (an R&D-intensive SME loses ERIS and falls back on the merged RDEC); a new SAO answerable for its arrangements; TP switching on.
>
> **Professional judgement.** Thresholds are measured on different numbers, from different accounts, over different periods. Write each test down with the source of each figure, so the SAO can rely on it, and review the map whenever the deal team is busy: the tax function is often the last to hear about a purchase and the first to be blamed for a missed deadline.

## How the paper is built

A brief word on the exam this book serves; chapter 32 owns the craft.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Paper | CTA Advanced Technical, Taxation of Larger Companies and Groups; renamed for 2023 from Taxation of Major Corporates |
| Duration and shape | 3 hours 30 minutes; normally six questions of 10, 15 or 20 marks; 100 marks; pass mark 50% (every paper M23–M26: usually three 20s, two 15s, one 10) |
| Syllabus | CT including CT on chargeable gains; capital allowances; stamp duty and SDLT at awareness level. At least **70%** of the CT element from core material |
| Grades | 1 core (depth, computation), 2 non-core (working knowledge), 3 awareness (recognition). In the 2026 grid most graded rows are core, including CFCs, TP, CIR and hybrids |
| Law | Kian's likely sitting, 4 May 2027 (fallback 26 October 2027), is expected to examine FA 2026; the 2027 grid and tax tables are not yet published |
| Scenarios | UK plc heading a multinational; foreign parent acquiring a UK company; JVs and consortia; overseas expansion by branch or subsidiary; group property reorganisations; disposals of subsidiaries; migration |
| Style | Technical prose and computations ("Calculate, with explanations", "Explain", "Discuss", occasionally "Recommend"); no letter, report or email format (that is the APS paper); 0.5–1 mark per point |
| Pass rates | M23 70%; N23 61%; M24 62%; N24 59%; M25 65%; N25 67%; M26 74%. The M24 chief examiner reported that Joint Programme candidates had the highest pass rates |
| Timing | About 2.1 minutes per mark (derived: 210 minutes ÷ 100 marks) |

> **Exam lens: reading a scenario for size and group**
> - **Grade:** the paper's 70% core rule means the computation and group topics dominate; awareness topics (Pillar Two, UTT, stamp taxes) earn add-on marks that are often missed.
> - **Method:** on any acquisition, disposal or restructuring, run two checks before writing: (1) which **guest lists** does each company join or leave? (2) which **rungs** does the group cross? Then list the consequences, each with authority, before going deep on any one. N24 Q5 is the model.
> - **Traps:** answering a different requirement (residence in a PE question; DPT for loans; hybrids with no trigger); "tax consequences" means all taxes in the syllabus, a named tax means only that tax; keep £ and £000 consistent.
> - Check the 2027 grid when it is published and correct any grade relied on here.

## What to take away

A company that joins a large group is still a separate taxpayer. *Salomon* confirmed that a company is a person distinct from its members, and corporation tax taxes that person: each company computes, files and pays its own tax, and there is no group return for corporation tax.

The law bridges the gap between the many companies and the one business with a toolkit of group regimes, **each with its own guest list**: associated companies (control; overseas companies count; dormant and passive holding companies ignored); the 51% group (GPAs, SSE, s 190 recovery, tax strategy and UTT); the 75% group with equity holder tests (group relief), and the consortium (5% members owning 75%); the gains group (75% plus effective 51%); stamp duty and SDLT groups (75% of shares, profits and assets, with arrangements tests); the worldwide group (CIR); consolidated groups for Pillar Two and CbC reporting.

**The consolidated tax charge is not the tax bill.** It includes overseas and deferred tax; the UK bill is a set of company liabilities.

**The ladder, for FY2026:** profits over £1.5m make a company large for QIPs, and over £20m very large, both divided by 1 + associated companies; net interest over £2m brings the CIR into play; £5m is the deductions allowance; £200m turnover or £2bn balance sheet switches on SAO, tax strategy and UTT; €750m switches on CbC reporting, TP records and Pillar Two; leaving the SME category switches on transfer pricing.

For Tarnmoor in GY1: revenue £1,180m (about €1,357m at the invented rate); a marginal relief divisor of 9 at once (limits £5,556 / £27,778); a QIP divisor of 8 for the 31 December companies (£187,500 / £2,500,000), because HMRC's manual counts associates on the day before the AP begins; and Calder still **large** in its first group AP (divisor 1: four instalments of £187,500 in months 7, 10, 13 and 16), becoming very large (divisor 9, £2,222,222) one period later.

And the job: identify the issues, explain them precisely, and coordinate the specialists.

To answer this chapter's question: Calder is **one company among many** for computing and paying its tax, and **part of one large group** for almost every threshold that decides how. Next, chapter 2 asks where all of these rules actually live, and how an adviser finds them.
