# Chapter nine: Buildings, fixtures, leasing and successions.

On 1 September in Group Year Three (GY3), Tarnmoor Engineering Ltd (TEL) takes the keys to a new distribution centre. Our invented group, Tarnmoor, is a listed engineering group, and everything about it in this book is made up for teaching. The building is brand new, bought from the developer who built it, for £5.2m. To the tax system it is at least three things, and possibly four.

The ground it stands on gets no allowance at all. The heating, the lighting and the electrical systems are plant, and they join a pool. The concrete, steel and roof are a structure, and they earn a slow, straight-line allowance that will outlive most of the people in the room.

This chapter is about the assets that sit between land and machinery, and about the moments when allowances move from one owner to another. It is the second capital allowances chapter in Part Two. Chapter 8 dealt with plant and machinery in the pools. Here we take the structures and buildings allowance (SBA) at Advanced Technical depth, then fixtures, long funding leases (LFLs), successions, contributions and the rules that stop allowances being bought and sold. Almost every topic here is **core** on the LCG syllabus; allowance buying and freeport special tax sites are **awareness** only. *The Living Law* (TKS), chapter 12, taught the basics of plant, pools and the SBA. We build on it.

**Abbreviations.** CAA 2001 = Capital Allowances Act 2001 (spoken "the Capital Allowances Act"); TCGA 1992 = Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 ("the Gains Act"); CTA 2010 = Corporation Tax Act 2010 ("the twenty ten Act"). All law is the law for **FY2026** (1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027) after Finance Act 2026. FA 2026 left the SBA, fixtures and LFLs unchanged; its 14% main pool WDA (FA 2026 s 28) matters here because fixtures and leased plant often land in the main pool.

---

## One building, four tax assets.

Start with the price. A building purchase contract usually gives one figure; the tax rules need it split, because each piece follows a different regime. Where property is sold together, the price is apportioned on a **just and reasonable** basis, whatever the parties call each part (CAA 2001 s 562). A contractual label does not bind HMRC if it is not just and reasonable.

| Piece | Examples | Tax treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Land | The site; rights over land | No allowance. SBA expressly excludes land acquisition costs (s 270BG); HMRC's manual (CA94010) adds that fees and SDLT relating to the land are excluded. Base cost for gains only |
| Structure | Walls, floors, roof, foundations, car parks, roads, bridges | SBA at 3% a year (Part 2A) |
| Fixtures that are plant | Integral features (s 33A: electrical and lighting systems, cold water, space or water heating, powered ventilation, air cooling and others); other fixed plant (sprinklers, racking bolted down) | P&M allowances: integral features to the **special rate pool** (6%); other plant usually to the **main pool** (14%) |
| Everything else | Land alteration (reclamation, remediation, landscaping that does not create a structure) | Nothing |

People assume that buying a building means buying allowances. Often it means buying allowances only on the parts the law recognises, only if the paperwork is right, and only at the rate the law sets for each piece. **A building is a bundle of tax assets, and the bundle is only as good as its weakest document.**

For TEL's distribution centre, the developer's price is split in our invented case as follows (a surveyor's report supports the split as just and reasonable):

| Component | £ |
|---|---|
| Land | 1,200,000 |
| Integral features | 600,000 |
| Structure | 3,400,000 |
| **Total price** | **5,200,000** |

---

## Why buildings got an allowance again.

For years before 2018, most new commercial buildings in the UK earned no capital allowance: a company could claim for the machines inside a factory and for some fixtures, but the shell was relieved only on sale, against a gain. The Budget of 29 October 2018 filled that gap with the SBA.

- **Start date.** The SBA is available only where the construction contract was entered into on or after **29 October 2018** (CAA 2001 s 270AB). If any contract for the physical construction predates it, the building does not qualify at all.
- **Rate.** 2% a year originally; **3% from 1 April 2020** for companies (6 April 2020 for income tax), so the allowance now runs for **33⅓ years** (s 270AA).
- **Three design ideas.** (1) A straight-line allowance on original qualifying cost, not a pool: no balancing allowance or charge on sale. (2) The allowance belongs to the building: a buyer carries on claiming the same annual amount for the rest of the 33⅓ years. (3) Clawback is through the **gains** computation: the seller adds the SBA it claimed to its disposal consideration (TCGA 1992 s 37B; GOV.UK: "add the total amount of structures and buildings allowance you've claimed to your disposal receipts").
- **Non-residential use.** Dwellings and residential use are excluded. A period of disuse after qualifying use does not stop the allowance; a switch to residential use does.
- **Allowance period start.** The later of (a) the date the building is first brought into non-residential use and (b) the date the qualifying expenditure is incurred.
- **Older buildings.** A building constructed under pre-29 October 2018 contracts earns nothing, but **capital expenditure on later alterations, extensions or renovations** can qualify in its own right if contracted for after the start date. The May 2026 paper tested exactly this with an office built in 2010: many candidates gave SBA on the whole office; only the alterations qualified.

**TEL's GY2 extension (invented).** TEL's GY2 capital allowances (£16.0m in total, chapter 8) include SBA on a **£1.96m extension** to an older factory, contracted for after the start date and in use throughout GY2: 3% × £1,960,000 = **£58,800**. The older factory earns nothing.

---

## What qualifies, and what does not.

**Construction by the claimant.** Qualifying expenditure is the capital cost of construction. Site preparation counts, and HMRC's manual treats demolition of an existing building to clear the site as site preparation. Excluded: land; land alteration (other than site preparation); plant (which qualifies under Part 2 instead); planning permission costs.

**Purchases.** Three rules (and the examiner likes them):

| Building bought | Qualifying expenditure for the buyer | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Unused, from a **developer** (sold in the course of its development trade) | The **price paid** for the relevant interest, apportioned to exclude land and non-structure items; if there were further sales before first use, the lower of the last buyer's price and the developer's sale price | CAA 2001 s 270BD; CA93650 |
| Unused, from a **non-developer** | **Lower of** the price paid and the original construction expenditure | s 270BC; CA93500 |
| **Used** (after first use) | No relief on the price. The buyer steps into the seller's shoes and claims 3% of the **original** qualifying expenditure for the rest of the period, if it has an **allowance statement** | Part 2A; GOV.UK guidance |

HMRC's guidance adds that if a buyer pays more than market value, the claim is limited to market value.

> **Worked example: buying a used building (hypothetical, not a story fact)**
> A warehouse cost £2,000,000 to construct (post-October 2018 contract). A buyer later pays £3,000,000, of which £800,000 is land.
>
> | | £ |
> |---|---|
> | Original qualifying expenditure | 2,000,000 |
> | Buyer's SBA a year (3%) | **60,000** |
> | Price paid for the structure (irrelevant to SBA) | 2,200,000 |
>
> The buyer claims £60,000 a year for the remaining period, not 3% of £2.2m.

**Demolition.** HMRC's manual: where the **whole** building is demolished it ceases to qualify, any unclaimed allowance is lost, and allowances already claimed are added to the consideration in the gains computation. Partial demolition is different: restoration works are new capital expenditure under the renovation and conversion provisions.

**Time apportionment.** The allowance is an annual amount, proportionately reduced for a period shorter than a year or for part-period qualifying use (s 270AA). Exam answers work to the nearest month ("All workings should be shown and made to the nearest month and pound unless the question specifies otherwise"). In November 2025 (Q4), faced with a new company's short first period, some candidates cut SBA to 1/9th of 3% a month instead of 1/12th. **The annual figure is the starting point; a month is always a twelfth of it.**

> **Exam lens: SBA**
> - **Grade:** "Buildings and structures allowances" **1 (core)** (2026 grid; check the 2027 grid when published).
> - **Past appearances:** M26 Q2 (15 marks: warehouse bought from a developer on the price paid excluding land and integral features; office built in 2010 where only alterations qualified, not planning permission); M25 Q4 (20 marks: SBA on second-hand buildings with conversion costs; the examiners found SBA qualifying expenditure weak); N25 Q4 (20 marks: SBA time-apportioned, 1/12th not 1/9th); M23 Q1 (20 marks: SBA on a new factory in a CT computation); N23 Q3(b) (CAs/SBA on a training facility: land, levelling, buildings).
> - **Style:** computations with explanations; 0.5–1 mark per point; conventional CA layout with SBA shown separately from the pools.
> - **Traps:** SBA on land, land alteration or integral features; SBA on a pre-29 October 2018 building beyond its alterations; using the price paid for a used building; months wrongly counted; forgetting the gains add-back on sale.

## Tarnmoor's distribution centre.

TEL buys and pays for the distribution centre on **1 September GY3** and first uses it the same day, so the allowance period starts then. TEL's year ends on 31 December: 4 months of qualifying use in GY3.

> **Worked example: TEL's distribution centre (story, GY3)**
>
> | | £ |
> |---|---|
> | Price paid to developer | 5,200,000 |
> | Less: land (no allowance) | (1,200,000) |
> | Less: integral features (P&M, special rate) | (600,000) |
> | **SBA qualifying expenditure (s 270BD)** | **3,400,000** |
> | SBA a year: 3% × £3,400,000 | 102,000 |
> | **GY3 SBA: £102,000 × 4/12** | **34,000** |
> | GY4 onwards (full year) | 102,000 |
> | Total over 33⅓ years | 3,400,000 |
>
> *Check by days (for interest only): £102,000 × 122/365 = £34,093. The exam convention (months) gives £34,000, the figure used in this book.*

**The integral features (£600,000).** These are special rate expenditure. Do they also earn the **50% special rate FYA** (CAA 2001 s 45S; chapter 8)? That needs the plant to be **unused and not second-hand**. Fixtures in a new building bought straight from the developer arguably meet the test, because nobody has used them, but no HMRC statement settling the point for fixtures in a building bought from a developer was found in the research for this chapter. In our invented case the tax team logs the question and the computation takes the cautious route:

| Integral features, GY3 | Cautious (no FYA) £ | If the 50% FYA is available £ |
|---|---|---|
| 50% FYA | — | 300,000 |
| Addition to special rate pool | 600,000 | 300,000 |
| WDA 6% on this addition in GY3 | 36,000 | nil (the balance joins the pool after the WDA: CAA 2001 s 58(5)) |
| **Allowances on the £600,000 in GY3** | **36,000** | **300,000** |

(Special rate WDAs are not time-apportioned for part-year ownership within a 12-month period. Where an FYA is claimed, the balance is pooled only after the WDA of the period of expenditure, so it first draws 6% in GY4.)

**No fixtures requirements here.** The developer held the building as trading stock: it never incurred capital expenditure on the fixtures and was never entitled to allowances on them. The pooling and fixed value requirements (ss 187A–187B, below) apply only where a **past owner was entitled to claim**. Buying new from a developer avoids them; the split is governed only by s 562.

**The gains thread.** Chapter 16 tells how Tarnmoor Estates Ltd (TES) sells its depot on 30 April GY3 for £6.0m and rolls part of the gain into this distribution centre: proceeds not reinvested £0.8m chargeable; £1,477,500 rolled over; **TEL's base cost £3,722,500**. When TEL eventually sells, every pound of SBA claimed is added to its disposal consideration. So the SBA is a deduction now against trading profits at 25%, matched by a larger gain later, which may itself be rolled over, covered by capital losses, or never realised. That timing advantage is the real value of the SBA to a group that holds buildings for decades.

---

## The allowance statement and the life of a building.

Because the allowance travels with the building, each new owner needs facts it cannot easily discover. The law answers with the **allowance statement** (CAA 2001 s 270IA).

- **No statement, no claim.** The person who incurred the expenditure must make one; a later buyer must obtain a copy from a past owner.
- **Contents:** a written statement identifying the building, and stating (a) the date of the **earliest contract for construction**, (b) the **amount of qualifying expenditure**, (c) the date the building was **first brought into non-residential use**, and (d) where further qualifying expenditure is incurred after that date, the date it is incurred (item (d) added by FA 2022 for expenditure from Royal Assent). Where the expenditure includes special tax site qualifying expenditure, the statement must show that amount separately (s 270IA(5)).
- Think of it as the building's **birth certificate**: lose it, and a later owner cannot prove the allowance life that is left.

**Due diligence.** On buying a used building: obtain the allowance statement, warranties that no construction contract predates 29 October 2018, and the seller's records of claims. On buying a company that owns buildings, ask the same questions inside the target. On selling, pass on the statement: a buyer who cannot claim will pay less.

**Life cycle.** On a sale the allowance for the year is apportioned between seller and buyer, and the buyer continues at the same annual amount; the seller adds its claims to its gains consideration. Demolition ends the allowance permanently.

> **Worked example: the seller's gain (hypothetical, not a story fact)**
> A company built a warehouse for £2,000,000 on land bought for £800,000 (all after December 2017, so no indexation). It claims £60,000 a year for 5 years and then sells for £3,000,000.
>
> | | £ |
> |---|---|
> | Disposal proceeds | 3,000,000 |
> | Add: SBA claimed (5 × £60,000) (TCGA 1992 s 37B) | 300,000 |
> | Deemed consideration | 3,300,000 |
> | Less: cost (land £800,000 + building £2,000,000) | (2,800,000) |
> | **Chargeable gain** | **500,000** |
>
> The allowances are **added to proceeds**, not deducted from cost. The buyer continues at £60,000 a year.

This is why the SBA behaves so differently from plant allowances: a pool claws back excess relief through a balancing charge taxed as income; a building claws it back through the gain, which may be rolled over or covered by capital losses.

> **Going further: the SBA in deferred tax and in groups**
> - **Intra-group transfers.** A building moving between group companies at no gain, no loss (TCGA 1992 s 171) still carries its SBA: the transferee continues at 3% of the original cost and needs the allowance statement. Do not confuse the gains base cost (transferor's cost) with the SBA base (original qualifying expenditure).
> - **Deferred tax (chapter 6).** The SBA creates a temporary difference between the carrying amount of the building and its tax base; the land usually creates none.
> - **Pricing.** A buyer of a used building values the remaining SBA stream (and its clawback for the seller) in the price; a seller who has claimed SBA should model the add-back before agreeing a sale price.

---

## Fixtures, and who owns what is fixed.

A **fixture** is plant or machinery so installed or fixed in or to a building or other land that it becomes, in law, part of that building or land (CAA 2001 Part 2 Ch 14, from s 172). Lifts, heating, air conditioning, wiring and sanitary fittings are classic examples.

Fixtures raise a problem ordinary plant does not. A machine moves with its buyer; a fixture belongs in law to whoever owns the land, which may be held by a freeholder, let, sublet, mortgaged and sold while the same boiler sits in the basement. Without special rules, several people could claim for one boiler, or none could.

- **Ownership rules (ss 176–184)** decide who is treated as owning a fixture: broadly, the person with an interest in the land who incurred the expenditure.
- **Ceasing to own (ss 188–192A)** and the **disposal value** table (s 196): on a sale of the qualifying interest, the seller's disposal value is normally the part of the sale price attributable to the fixtures.
- **Past-owner cap (s 185):** if a past owner claimed and brought a disposal value into account, the new owner's qualifying expenditure is capped at that disposal value (plus s 25 installation costs). It stops a fixture growing in value for tax as it passes from hand to hand.

**Analogy.** Fixtures are like luggage on a journey with connecting flights. Checked through properly at each change, it arrives with every passenger who comes after. If one owner fails to check it through, it is lost for every later owner too. The precise rule is the pooling requirement and the fixed value requirement (next section).

Two practical points for a group:
1. Integral features go to the **special rate pool**; other fixtures to the **main pool**. A landlord company such as TES can claim on fixtures in commercial buildings it lets, because a property business is a qualifying activity (s 15); allowances are given effect against the property business, with any excess added to management expenses (s 253; CTA 2009 s 1233).
2. Fixtures are plant, so they can attract the **AIA** even when second-hand; **full expensing and the 50% FYA cannot** be claimed on second-hand fixtures (s 45S: unused and not second-hand).

---

## The pooling and fixed value requirements.

Before 2012, a seller could claim on fixtures for years, sell the building without a meaningful disposal value, and leave the buyer to claim again on its own valuation of the same fixtures: two claims on one boiler. Parliament closed this in two steps:

| Requirement | Applies from | Met if | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed value** (where the past owner must bring in a disposal value under s 196 items 1, 5 or 9) | 1 April 2012 | Within **2 years** of the transfer, a joint **s 198/s 199 election**, or an application to the **tribunal** to fix the value (or the statements route for intervening non-claimants) | s 187A |
| **Pooling** | **1 April 2014** (CT) | The past owner allocated the expenditure to a pool, or claimed an FYA on it, in a chargeable period beginning on or before the day it ceased to own the fixture | s 187A |
| **Disposal value statement** (other s 196 cases; s 61 item 7) | — | A written statement within 2 years | s 187A |

The law says that where a **past owner was entitled to claim** on the fixture, a buyer's new expenditure is treated as **nil** unless the requirements are met, and the nil carries through to every later owner whose title passes through it. The **burden** of showing the requirements were met is on the current owner (s 187B). In practice: copies of the seller's computations and the signed election.

**Misconception: "a property buyer can always claim allowances on the fixtures it buys."** Wrong. A buyer can claim only if the seller pooled and the value was fixed within 2 years. If the seller never claimed although entitled to, the buyer may claim nothing. The exception is where no past owner was ever entitled to claim (for example a developer holding the building as trading stock): then ss 187A–187B do not bite. A buyer who wants allowances must make them a condition of the deal before exchange; after completion, the seller has no reason to help.

---

## The section 198 election.

The tool for meeting the fixed value requirement is the joint election in **CAA 2001 s 198** (s 199 is its twin on the **grant of a lease**).

- **Joint:** made by seller and buyer.
- **Effect:** fixes the part of the sale price attributable to the fixtures. It is the seller's disposal value and the buyer's qualifying expenditure. The balance of the price is the price of the rest of the property.
- **Cap:** cannot exceed the seller's original qualifying expenditure on the fixtures, or the actual price.
- **Irrevocable;** made within **2 years** of the sale (GOV.UK guidance).

**The negotiation.** The seller wants a **low** figure (smaller pool reduction, no balancing charge); the buyer wants a **high** figure (more qualifying expenditure). Every pound moved is a pound of allowances moved from one side to the other. A common outcome is a figure that leaves the seller with no balancing charge, with the price adjusted to compensate.

> **Worked example: TES's office fixtures (story, GY2)**
> TES buys an office building in GY2. The seller's original qualifying expenditure on the fixtures was **£700,000**. A s 198 election fixes the fixtures at **£400,000** (within the cap: lower than £700,000 and than the price). The fixtures are all integral features.
>
> | TES, GY2 | Special rate pool £ |
> |---|---|
> | Addition: s 198 elected value | 400,000 |
> | AIA | (400,000) |
> | c/f | nil |
>
> The group allocates £400,000 of its single £1m AIA to TES (chapter 8: the AIA for the year to 31 March GY3), so the whole £400,000 is relieved at once. Without the AIA, the 6% WDA would have given only £24,000 in GY2, leaving £376,000 in the pool.

**The gains trap.** The election does **not** change the gains computation. TES's base cost is the **whole price** paid for the office, including the fixtures element; on a sale, the **whole price** is the proceeds. The examiners reported after M23 (Q4) that candidates deducted fixtures amounts from gains computations, and the N25 (Q5) report stressed that CA-claimed expenditure adjusts the gains computation only where there is a loss. The only interaction is the **loss restriction** for capital allowances (TCGA 1992 s 41): an allowable loss is restricted by the net allowances given.

> **Worked example: the loss restriction (hypothetical figures, TES's office)**
> Suppose TES paid £3,000,000 for the office (no indexation: bought after December 2017) and has had allowances of £400,000 on the fixtures.
>
> | | Sale at £3.6m £ | Sale at £2.5m £ |
> |---|---|---|
> | Proceeds (whole price, including fixtures element) | 3,600,000 | 2,500,000 |
> | Less: cost (whole price) | (3,000,000) | (3,000,000) |
> | Unadjusted gain / (loss) | 600,000 | (500,000) |
> | Restriction: net allowances (£400,000 claimed less £100,000 disposal value fixed by a new s 198 election) | n/a (gain) | 300,000 |
> | **Chargeable gain / (allowable loss)** | **600,000** | **(200,000)** |
>
> The figure for "net allowances" is stated broadly (allowances given less the disposal value brought into the pool).

> **Exam lens: fixtures**
> - **Grade:** "Fixtures" **1 (core)**.
> - **Past appearances:** M23 Q4 (20 marks: property, factory hived down, **s 198 elections**, group roll-over; candidates deducted fixtures amounts from gains computations); N25 Q5 (20 marks: group property, intra-group NGNL transfer, refurbishment with integral features, **s 198 joint election**, SDLT, roll-over; only a minority dealt with CAs and the fixtures election); M26 Q4 (fixtures disposal value in a property question).
> - **Traps:** fixtures values deducted from gains; forgetting the pooling and fixed value requirements on a second-hand building; elected value above the seller's original cost; forgetting that a developer seller means no s 198 election is needed (or possible).
> - **Layout:** the elected figure enters the CA columns (special rate or main pool), never the gains computation (except the loss restriction).

## Long funding leases, where allowances follow the economics.

Leasing raises a different question: when one company owns a machine and another uses it, who gets the allowances? Historically the owner, meaning the lessor. Lessors with taxable profits bought plant, claimed the allowances and passed part of the benefit to lessees in lower rentals. The largest deals ended in court.

The best known is ***Barclays Mercantile Business Finance Ltd v Mawson*** [2004] UKHL 51. BMBF paid about £91m for part of a gas pipeline under the Irish Sea and leased it back to Bord Gáis Éireann. The Revenue's case was that the payment produced no real commercial benefit and existed mainly to generate allowances; the House of Lords held that the lessor had incurred the expenditure and was entitled to the allowances. (Facts from secondary reports; the judgment was not opened for this chapter.)

In **FA 2006 (Sch 8, inserting CAA 2001 Part 2 Ch 6A)** Parliament changed the question for **long funding leases**: the allowances move from lessor to **lessee**, on the idea that a lease that really finances the purchase of an asset should be taxed like a loan. The lessor is taxed on its finance return and claims nothing (CTA 2010 Part 9).

| Test | Rule | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Long funding lease | A **funding lease** that is not a **short lease**, not an excluded lease of background plant for a building (s 70R), and not excluded by s 70U (plant leased with land) | CAA 2001 s 70G |
| Funding lease | Meets at least one test at inception: (a) **finance lease test**: under GAAP it is (or would be) a finance lease or loan (s 70N); (b) **lease payments test**: PV of minimum lease payments (at the implicit rate) ≥ **80%** of fair value (s 70O); (c) **useful economic life test**: term > **65%** of remaining useful economic life (s 70P) | s 70J |
| Short lease | Term of **7 years or less**, with anti-avoidance for linked leases and leasebacks | s 70I |
| Lessee's return | For the lessee it is an LFL only if its **tax return for the initial period treats it as one**; not correctable by an error or mistake claim | s 70H |
| Right-of-use lessees | An RoU lease that is an LFL meeting the s 70O or s 70P test is a long funding **finance** lease for the lessee | s 70YI |

**The lessee's position.** The lessee is treated as owning the plant and incurring capital expenditure at the start of the term (s 70A): for a long funding operating lease the amount is set by s 70B, for a long funding finance lease by s 70C (broadly, the present value of the minimum lease payments recognised in the accounts: HMRC BLM42010). In return, the lessee's deduction for rentals under a long funding **finance** lease is capped at the **finance charge** under GAAP (CTA 2010 s 377; s 377A for RoU remeasurements); under a long funding **operating** lease, deductions are reduced by the time-apportioned expected fall in value (s 379).

---

## Tarnmoor's machine on a lease.

In our invented case, from **1 January GY3**, TEL takes a large, **refurbished (previously used)** computer-controlled machining centre on a **10-year finance lease** from an unconnected leasing company. PV of the minimum lease payments: **£1,500,000**; rentals £203,802 a year in arrears; implicit rate 6%.

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Finance lease test (s 70N) | Met: the accounts treat it as a finance lease, so a funding lease |
| Short lease (s 70I) | No: 10 years > 7 |
| Excluded (s 70R, s 70U) | No |
| Lessee's return (s 70H) | TEL's GY3 return treats it as an LFL |
| **Result** | **LFL: TEL (lessee) claims; the lessor claims nothing** |

> **Worked example: TEL's LFL (story, GY3)**
>
> | Capital allowances | Main pool £ |
> |---|---|
> | Addition: deemed expenditure (s 70A/70C) | 1,500,000 |
> | FYA | nil: second-hand, so no full expensing (s 45S) and no 40% FYA (s 45U) |
> | WDA 14% attributable to this addition | 210,000 |
>
> | Profit adjustments, GY3 | £ |
> |---|---|
> | Rental paid (annuity: £1,500,000 × 0.06 / (1 − 1.06⁻¹⁰)) | 203,802 |
> | Deductible: finance charge (6% × £1,500,000) (CTA 2010 s 377) | 90,000 |
> | Not deductible: capital element (relieved by allowances) | 113,802 |
> | Depreciation of the asset in the accounts | added back |

**Examiner's angle.** N25 Q1 (20 marks) included "machinery on long funded lease"; the suggested answer put it in the **main pool**, and the examiners listed "treating the long-funding lease as special rate expenditure (rather than an addition to the main pool)" as a common error. LFL plant goes in the pool its own nature dictates.

**Open question: full expensing for an LFL lessee of new plant.** The Act contains an express bar on AIA and FYAs for **transfer and long funding leaseback** arrangements (CAA 2001 s 70DA; BLM62110). No express bar was found for an ordinary LFL of new plant, and secondary commentary (KPMG) says a lessee treated as tax owner can claim FYAs if the other conditions are met. The N25 suggested answer gave main pool WDAs without discussing the point. **This is not settled in the sources checked.** In an exam, follow the facts, state your assumption and move on. The story avoids the question by making TEL's machine second-hand.

> **Exam lens: long funding leases**
> - **Grade:** "Long funding leases" **1 (core)** in the CA section, and "Leasing plant and machinery – long funding leases only" **1** in the CT section (2026 grid). The 2028 grid drops leases; Kian's 2027 sitting keeps them core.
> - **Past appearance:** N25 Q1 (LFL machinery in the main pool; error: special rate).
> - **Traps:** a lease of 7 years or less is a short lease (not an LFL); the lessee, not the lessor, claims; rentals deductible only to the extent of the finance charge; the return must treat it as an LFL.

> **Going further: leases and the tax function**
> - Classify every plant lease at inception (term, finance lease test, 80% and 65% tests) and record the classification: the s 70H choice cannot be corrected later.
> - Map lease accounting (FRS 101/IFRS 16 right-of-use assets) to tax: the depreciation add-back, the finance charge deduction, the CA addition.
> - Chapter 28 explains how lease finance charges are treated in the corporate interest restriction.

## Successions, when a business changes hands.

When one person succeeds to another's qualifying activity, the plant passes with it (CAA 2001 ss 265–268).

- **General rule (s 265):** the plant is treated as sold at **market value** at the date of succession. The predecessor brings market value into its pool as a disposal value (balancing adjustments in its final period). The successor's expenditure is market value, with **no AIA and no FYA**. Without that bar, a business could be passed around to refresh allowances on old plant.
- **Was there a succession?** A question of fact. Tribunals still use Widgery J's test in ***Kenmir Ltd v Frizzell*** [1968] 1 All ER 414 at 418: "the vital consideration is whether the effect of the transaction was to put the transferee in possession of a going concern…", quoted by the FTT in ***Haymarket Media Group Ltd v HMRC*** [2022] UKFTT 168 (TC) (Judge Heidi Poon and Julian Sims; a VAT transfer of a going concern case on the sale of the Teddington Studios site, appeal dismissed). *Kenmir* was an employment case: use it as the going concern test, not as capital allowances authority. Buying assets is not succeeding to a business.
- **Connected-party election (ss 266–267):** where predecessor and successor are **connected** (s 575 plus the extended tests in s 266(5)) and both are within the charge to UK tax on the activity, they may **jointly elect within 2 years** of the succession for the plant to pass at **tax written down value**: no balancing adjustment for the predecessor; the successor steps into its shoes. Not available to a **dual resident investing company**, or where **s 561** applies.

> **Worked example: market value or the election (hypothetical)**
>
> | Connected succession; plant TWDV £2,000,000; market value £3,000,000 | No election £ | s 266 election £ |
> |---|---|---|
> | Predecessor: disposal value | 3,000,000 | 2,000,000 |
> | Predecessor: balancing charge | 1,000,000 | nil |
> | Successor: qualifying expenditure | 3,000,000 (no AIA/FYA) | 2,000,000 (continues pools) |

**Inside a group: Part 22.** Where a trade passes between companies under common ownership, **CTA 2010 Part 22 Ch 1** can apply automatically; **s 948** then continues allowances as if the successor had always carried on the trade, and the transfer gives no allowances or charges. Chapter 19 owns Part 22. In our invented case, when TEL hives its actuators trade down into Tarnmoor Actuators Ltd (TAL) on **1 February GY6**, the plant passes at TWDV under s 948: no balancing charge, no election needed. (Where the cross-border rule in CAA 2001 s 561 applies, s 948 is disapplied.)

> **Exam lens: successions**
> - **Grade:** "Successions" **1 (core)**.
> - **Past appearances:** no standalone CA succession question M23–M26; M23 Q4 included a factory hived down with the trade (gains and Part 22 context). Expect it embedded in a reorganisation or acquisition question.
> - **Traps:** giving AIA or FYA to a successor; forgetting the 2-year joint election; using s 266 where Part 22 Ch 1 applies automatically; ignoring that a mere asset purchase is not a succession.

---

## Connected parties, cross-border transfers and the Act's toolbox.

**Connected sales of plant (ss 214, 217, 218).** A group company selling plant to a fellow group company is a connected-party transaction (s 575). The buyer gets **no AIA and no FYA** (s 217), and its qualifying expenditure is **capped at the seller's disposal value** (or, if none, the lower of market value and the original cost to the seller or a connected person) (s 218). The aim: no fresh allowances from selling plant to yourself at a high price.

**Non-P&M Parts (ss 567–570).** Where buyer and seller are under common control, or the sole or main benefit of the sale is a tax advantage, the sale is treated as at **market value** (ss 567–568). Where control is the only reason and there is no tax advantage, the parties may elect for the **alternative amount** (broadly the lower of market value and the unrelieved balance) (s 569); barred where the buyer is a **dual resident investing company** (s 570). These sections do not apply to Part 2 (P&M) or where s 561 applies; within the syllabus they matter mainly for R&D allowances (chapter 10). **s 570A** denies a balancing allowance where a tax avoidance scheme has reduced the proceeds.

**Cross-border transfers (ss 561, 561A).** s 561 applies to a transfer within TCGA 1992 s 140A between qualifying companies ("relevant state" = the UK or a member State, s 561(4A)), where the transferee is UK resident or carries on the business through a UK PE: **no allowances or charges**, and the transferee **stands in the transferor's shoes** (CTA 2010 s 948 then disapplied). s 561A covers cross-border mergers (TCGA s 140E). These rules were built for EU law; **how far TCGA s 140A's conditions still operate after Brexit is unclear**. In an exam, recognise them, state the effect, and note that the conditions turn on the definition of a relevant state.

**Apportionment (s 562)** and **final provisions (ss 571–581)**: the Act's toolbox of definitions, including transfers treated as sales (s 573) and connected persons (s 575). They answer three questions every transaction raises: was there a sale, at what price, and between whom?

> **Exam lens: transfers, miscellaneous and final provisions**
> - **Grades:** "Transfers – s.561, 561A CAA 2001" **1**; "Miscellaneous – s.562–570A" **1**; "Final provisions – s.571–581" **1** (all core in the 2026 grid).
> - **Past appearances:** not examined as standalone questions M23–M26; connected-party sales and apportionment appear inside property and reorganisation questions.
> - **Traps:** AIA/FYA on a connected purchase; a price above the seller's disposal value; forgetting the just and reasonable apportionment when the contract allocates artificially.

---

## Contributions and grants.

Capital allowances relieve the cost a business bears.

| Rule | Detail | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| General rule | Expenditure is treated as **not incurred** by a person to the extent it is met, directly or indirectly, by a **public body** or **another person**. Applies across the Act, including the SBA | CAA 2001 s 532 |
| Insurance and compensation | Outside the general rule | s 535 |
| Non-relievable contributor | Where the contributor is not a public body and cannot get allowances or a deduction for its contribution, the **recipient is treated as incurring the expenditure** | s 536 |
| Contribution allowances | A contributor paying towards another's capital expenditure for its **own** trade or other qualifying activity can claim allowances as if it owned the asset, **if not connected** with the recipient | ss 537–538 |
| SBA version | Contribution allowances adapted for Part 2A | s 538A |

**The group consequence.** Group companies are connected, so a group company that pays towards a fellow member's building gets **no contribution allowance**; because it cannot claim, s 536 leaves the allowances with the recipient. For a group, that is usually the right place for them.

> **Worked example: TES's flood wall (story, GY3)**
> In GY3 TES builds a concrete flood wall protecting a riverside site it lets to TEL. Cost **£500,000**; in qualifying use from **1 January GY3**. The local authority (a public body) pays a grant of **£200,000**.
>
> | | £ |
> |---|---|
> | Cost of the wall | 500,000 |
> | Less: local authority grant (s 532) | (200,000) |
> | **SBA qualifying expenditure** | **300,000** |
> | **SBA a year (3%), full year in GY3** | **9,000** |
>
> Chapter 28 returns to the grant in the corporate interest restriction.

> **Exam lens: contributions**
> - **Grade:** "Contributions" **1 (core)**. Not seen as a standalone question M23–M26; expect a line in a CA computation (a grant towards plant or a building).
> - **Traps:** claiming on the gross cost when a public grant has been received; giving a contribution allowance to a connected contributor.

---

## Anti-avoidance and the special tax sites.

**Allowance buying (awareness).** A company whose plant has a tax written down value above its balance sheet value holds latent allowances that a buyer with profits might exploit. **FA 2010 (s 26, Sch 4)** inserted **CAA 2001 Part 2 Ch 16A (ss 212A–212S)**, effective from **21 July 2009**. It applies where there is a **qualifying change** in ownership (s 212C) of a company with a **relevant excess of allowances** (TWDV above balance sheet value, ss 212J–212L) and a **limiting condition** is met (s 212LA, FA 2013): excess **£50m or more**; excess **£2m or more** and not insignificant relative to the benefits of the change; or a smaller excess where the change has an **unallowable purpose** (s 212M); or arrangements to keep below the thresholds. FA 2013 also renamed the Chapter "restrictions on allowance buying" and extended it to all qualifying activities. When the rules bite, the excess is restricted so that the change of ownership cannot be used to put it to work for the new owners (detailed mechanics, ss 212N–212S, not opened for this chapter). CTA 2010 Part 9 separately deals with sales of lessor companies. **Pattern to recognise:** tax value above book value plus a change of ownership.

**Freeports and investment zones: special tax sites (awareness).**
- **P&M:** 100% FYA for companies on unused plant for use **primarily** in a special tax site, in a trade, incurred by the site's sunset date (CAA 2001 ss 45O–45R); the plant must remain primarily in use in the site for **5 years** (s 45R).
- **SBA:** an enhanced **10% a year over 10 years** for special tax site qualifying expenditure (s 270AA(2A), (5)).
- **Sunset dates:** GOV.UK guidance gives the enhanced SBA for expenditure up to **30 September 2031** for English freeport tax sites and **30 September 2034** for Scottish Green Freeports, Welsh Freeports and Investment Zones (the building must also be brought into qualifying use by then). The original date was 30 September 2026. The government's policy paper extending the sunset dates gives the same new dates for the special tax site reliefs generally, including the plant FYA; reliefs vary by investment zone, so check the site's designation before use.
- Tarnmoor has no freeport site. In an exam, a scenario that mentions a freeport invites a line on these reliefs.

> **Exam lens: avoidance and freeports**
> - **Grades:** "Avoidance involving allowance buying and other anti-avoidance" **3 (awareness)**; "Freeports" **3 (awareness)**.
> - **Past appearances:** none M23–M26.
> - **Style:** recognition and a brief statement of the rule; no computation expected.

---

## The tax function's checklist, and the examiner's.

> **Going further: the checklist**
>
> | Transaction | Questions | Deadline |
> |---|---|---|
> | Buying a building | Just and reasonable split (s 562): land, structure, integral features, other plant, non-qualifying; developer, non-developer or used (s 270BC–270BE); allowance statement and contract-date warranties; seller pooled? s 198 election | s 198: 2 years from the sale; but negotiate before exchange |
> | Selling a building | SBA add-back to gains consideration; fixtures disposal value; pass on the allowance statement | Same s 198 deadline |
> | Leasing plant | LFL classification at inception; return treatment (s 70H); rentals limited to the finance charge | The return for the initial period |
> | Reorganisations | Succession (s 265), Part 22 (s 948) or connected sale (ss 214–218)? Use s 266 where it helps | s 266: 2 years from the succession |
> | Grants and contributions | Net public grants (s 532); connected contributors get no allowance (s 537) | — |
> | Intra-group property transfers (e.g. Calder's works to TES, the water-systems factory to TWS in GY3) | Fixtures: connected sale (no AIA/FYA; cap); s 198 election between the group companies; SBA continues with the statement | 2 years |

**How the examiner tests this chapter.** Usually embedded in a larger question: M26 Q2 (warehouse from a developer; 2010 office with alterations), M25 Q4 (second-hand buildings with conversion costs), N25 Q4 (time apportionment by twelfths), M23 Q4 and N25 Q5 (fixtures elections; fixtures values wrongly deducted from gains; few dealt with the election), N25 Q1 (LFL in the main pool). Answers are technical prose with computations in the conventional CA columns (FYA/FE, main pool, special rate pool, single asset pools, allowances, with SBA shown separately); never letters or reports. Keep £ and £000 consistent within each table.

---

## What to take away.

- A building is a bundle of tax assets: land (nothing), structure (SBA), integral features and other fixtures (P&M). A just and reasonable apportionment (s 562) splits the price, whatever the contract says.
- **SBA:** 3% a year of qualifying construction cost for 33⅓ years from the later of first non-residential use and the expenditure; construction contract on or after 29 October 2018; older buildings: only later alterations and extensions. Land, land alteration and plant excluded. Bought unused from a developer: price paid; unused from anyone else: lower of price and construction cost; used: 3% of the original cost continues. No balancing adjustment on sale; the seller adds its SBA to its gains consideration. Demolition ends it. No claim without an allowance statement.
- **TEL's distribution centre:** structure £3.4m, SBA £102,000 a year, **£34,000** for 4 months of GY3; land £1.2m nothing; integral features £0.6m to the special rate pool.
- **Fixtures:** a buyer claims only if the past owner pooled (from April 2014) and the value was fixed (from April 2012), usually by a joint **s 198 election** within 2 years, capped at the seller's original cost. Miss either and the claim is nil for every later owner. The election affects allowances, not gains (except the loss restriction). TES's office fixtures: **£400,000**, covered by the group AIA.
- **LFLs:** a funding lease (finance lease, 80% payments or 65% useful life test) of more than 7 years; the lessee claims on the PV of the payments and deducts only the finance charge. TEL's machine: **£1.5m** to the main pool.
- **Successions:** market value, no AIA/FYA (s 265), unless connected parties elect within 2 years for TWDV (ss 266–267), or Part 22 Ch 1 passes it at TWDV automatically (s 948). Connected plant sales: no AIA/FYA; cost capped at the seller's disposal value.
- **Contributions:** public grants reduce qualifying expenditure; connected contributors get no contribution allowance. TES's flood wall qualifies on **£300,000** (SBA £9,000 a year).
- **Awareness:** allowance buying (Ch 16A) and freeport special tax sites (100% FYA; 10% SBA).

Next, chapter 10 turns from buildings and machines to ideas, and to research and development.

# Chapter ten: Research and development.

*In our invented case*, it is a grey morning in early April of GY2, and Graham Pike, the finance director of Calder Valve Engineering Ltd (CVE), is reading a checklist from the group tax team. Calder is the invented valve maker from *The Living Law* (TKS), now owned by our invented group, Tarnmoor. Its first year inside the group has just ended on 31 March GY2. Calder has spent £2.0m developing a valve that can sense its own wear. Item four on the checklist asks a simple question: has Calder made a research and development claim in the last three years? Graham checks the files. Calder has never claimed at all.

That one fact sets a clock running. If Calder does not tell HMRC that it intends to claim within six months of the end of that period of account, the claim is invalid. Not reduced: invalid. A credit worth £400,000 would be lost for want of a short online form.

This chapter is about the relief that pays companies to invent, and the machinery around it, which is now as much about proof and procedure as about rates. It sits in Part Two (measuring profit) because the relief works inside the trading computation. All three syllabus rows it covers are **core (grade 1)**: the research and development expenditure credit, R&D intensive companies, and R&D allowances. *The Living Law*, chapter 21, introduced the merged scheme and ERIS at TKS level. Here we go deeper: the payment steps, group surrender, the size tests that catch a start-up the day a large group buys it, the overseas restriction, and the claim notification trap that Graham has just found.

The law is **FY2026** law under FA 2026. The main rules are in **CTA 2009 Part 13** (Chapter 1A, the merged RDEC, ss 1042A ff; Chapter 2, ERIS, ss 1044 ff; and the general provisions later in the Part) and the allowances in **CAA 2001 Part 6** (ss 437–451).

---

## Why the state pays for ideas.

When a company discovers something, it cannot keep all of the value. Competitors learn from its products, its engineers move on, and other firms build on what it has shown is possible. Economists call this a **positive externality**: the company bears the whole cost but captures only part of the benefit, so left alone it under-invests.

GOV.UK's guidance on the merged scheme gives the policy aim as "to support and incentivise R&D, helping overcome a market failure (positive externality) which causes underinvestment in R&D". The relief is a subsidy delivered through the tax system, and a large one. HMRC's *Research and Development Tax Credits Statistics* (September 2026) give a **provisional £8.2bn** of relief claimed for 2024–25, on about **40,325 claims**, down about **17%** in a year, driven by a fall of about 19% in SME claims (large company claims rose about 4%).

**Does it work?** An HMRC working paper (2015) estimated that each £1 of tax forgone stimulated **£1.53 to £2.35** of extra R&D spending. HMRC's evaluation of RDEC (published November 2020) put the figure for that scheme at **£2.40 to £2.70** per £1 of relief. Both count only extra spending by existing claimants (the "intensive margin"), not wider spillovers.

**The other side is abuse.** During the years of easy claims, a market grew up of advisers who promised refunds for routine work and took a percentage. HMRC revised its estimate of error and fraud for 2020–21 to **16.7%** of the cost of the reliefs (about **£1.13bn**), with **24.4%** in the old SME scheme. Later HMRC publications give lower figures for later years on different bases (for example 9.9% for 2022–23 in the HMRC Annual Report and Accounts 2024–25), which do not fully reconcile. Those numbers explain almost every procedural rule in this chapter: advance notification, the additional information form, the overseas restriction and the PAYE cap.

**The debate.** One side says R&D relief is among the most effective things the tax system does, and that complexity and compliance burdens deter the honest small firms who need it most. The other says a relief paid in cash to loss-making companies will attract fraud unless it is fenced, and that the fences are the price of keeping the relief. The law today reflects the second view tempered by the first. As a larger-company adviser you will meet both the group that under-claims because nobody joined up the engineers and the tax team, and the boutique adviser who offers to find a refund that is not there.

---

## What counts as research and development.

The tax definition starts from GAAP (the definition is aligned with ITA 2007 s 1006 and the regulations made under it) and is shaped by the government's *Guidelines on the Meaning of Research and Development for Tax Purposes*, which the definition adopts. The heart of the test is that a project **seeks an advance in science or technology** through the **resolution of scientific or technological uncertainty**. The Guidelines ask whether a **competent professional** in the field would regard the advance as one, rather than as routine. Work that applies known techniques, however clever or valuable commercially, is not R&D for tax.

**The cases.** Both recent decisions are First-tier Tribunal decisions and bind no one:

- *Get Onbord Ltd v HMRC* [2024] UKFTT 617 (TC): an AI tool for "know your client" checks. HMRC refused the claim, saying the project did not advance overall knowledge or capability. The **taxpayer won**. The tribunal accepted the company's evidence and said that once a taxpayer has shown enough to suggest an overall advance, HMRC must produce some material to show the advance was only routine (a point about the evidential burden, as reported by ICAEW).
- *Tills Plus Ltd v HMRC* [2024] UKFTT 614 (TC): a software project found to combine existing technology and products rather than to develop something new. The tribunal found no evidence of an advance achieved by resolving scientific or technological uncertainty, and **HMRC won**. Commentators noted that an expert report for the company lacked evidence and reasoning.

The lesson: the test is the same, and **evidence decides it**. A claim stands or falls on contemporaneous records showing what was uncertain, why a competent engineer could not look the answer up, and what the team tried.

**Project Ashlar (invented).** Calder's smart process valve carries sensors inside the valve body to measure vibration and seal wear, so that a refinery can replace a valve before it fails. Nobody knew whether sensors and wiring could survive the pressure and heat, or whether a signal could pass reliably through thick steel. Dan Hartley (TKS; invented), a chartered engineer, spends **60%** of his time on Ashlar in Calder's first group year (AP 1 April GY1 to 31 March GY2). His design notes and failed prototypes are exactly the evidence a tribunal looks for.

**Misconception (minor):** R&D need not happen in a laboratory. A workshop where a team cracks open a failed prototype qualifies if the project seeks a genuine advance; the shiniest laboratory does not qualify for routine testing of a known product.

---

## The merged expenditure credit.

For many years the UK ran two schemes: an enhanced deduction (with a payable credit for loss makers) for SMEs, and an above-the-line expenditure credit (RDEC) for larger companies. At the **Autumn Statement of 22 November 2023** the government announced a merger. **FA 2024 Sch 1** enacted the merged scheme and a separate enhanced relief for loss-making R&D-intensive SMEs, from an appointed day set by regulations (SI 2024/286): **accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024**.

| Feature | Merged scheme RDEC (CTA 2009 Part 13 Ch 1A) |
|---|---|
| Rate | **20%** of qualifying expenditure (s 1042G); 49% for ring fence trades (outside LCG) |
| Who | Any trading company, any size (including SMEs that are not R&D intensive) |
| Tax treatment | Taxable trading receipt of the AP (above the line) |
| Net value | 20% × (1 − 25%) = **15%** at the main rate; 20% × (1 − 19%) = **16.2%** at the small profits rate |
| Use | Seven payment steps (ss 1042I ff): own CT first, cash last |

Three features set the credit apart from the old enhanced deduction.

**First, the credit is taxable.** It is a trading receipt of the period. The company deducts its R&D spending in full as normal trading expenses and then adds the credit back as income. That is why it appears above the line, like a grant, and why it increases accounting profit before tax.

**Second, the net value is lower than the headline.** For a company paying 25%, a 20% credit is worth 20% less a quarter of itself: 15% of the spending. For a company taxed at 19%, the net value is 16.2%. On £1m of qualifying expenditure that is £150,000 or £162,000. Compare the ERIS ceiling below (£269,700 on £1m), which is why the size tests matter so much to a start-up.

**Third, the credit is used through fixed payment steps** that pay the company's own CT first and produce cash only at the end. Those steps are where the examiners have caught candidates, so we take them slowly below.

> **Worked example 10.1: Calder's first claim (AP 1 April GY1 to 31 March GY2) (invented)**
>
> | £ | |
> |---|---:|
> | Tax-EBITDA (before CAs and before RDEC) | 4,400,000 |
> | Less capital allowances (incl. R&D allowance £500,000; WE 10.4) | (1,800,000) |
> | Adjusted trading profit before RDEC (after deducting £2,000,000 R&D costs as normal expenses) | 2,600,000 |
> | Add RDEC: 20% × £2,000,000 (taxable trading receipt) | 400,000 |
> | **Taxable total profits** | **3,000,000** |
> | CT at 25% | 750,000 |
> | Step 1: RDEC discharges CT of the period | (400,000) |
> | **CT payable** | **350,000** |
>
> Net benefit to the group: £400,000 − (25% × £400,000) = **£300,000**, i.e. 15% of qualifying expenditure. Calder is large, not very large, in this AP (its associates are counted on 31 March GY1, when it had none: chapter 3), so it pays four instalments of £187,500 in months 7, 10, 13 and 16; the credit does not reduce them (CIRD89870).

---

## Qualifying expenditure.

The credit is 20% of qualifying expenditure, and the law lists the categories (CTA 2009 ss 1123 ff as applied by Ch 1A). A cost outside them does not count, however closely it relates to the project.

| Category | Rule | Calder AP to 31 March GY2 (£) |
|---|---|---:|
| Staffing costs | Salaries, employer's NIC and employer pension contributions of staff directly and actively engaged in R&D; partly engaged staff apportioned on a just and reasonable basis | Dan Hartley: 60% × £120,000 = **72,000**; other engineers and technicians 1,428,000; total **1,500,000** |
| Externally provided workers (EPWs) | Unconnected provider: **65%** of the payment; connected (or electing) providers: by reference to the provider's own relevant costs | — |
| Contractor payments (contracted-out R&D) | Unconnected contractor: **65%** of the relevant (UK or s 1138A) portion (CIRD138000); connected or jointly elected (s 1135): different measure | Brackenwell (unconnected throughout the AP): 65% × £400,000 = **260,000** |
| Consumable items | Materials used up or transformed in the R&D (prototype castings, seals, sensors) | **180,000** |
| Software, data licences and cloud computing | So far as used directly in the R&D (data and cloud from APs beginning on or after 1 April 2023) | **60,000** |
| **Qualifying expenditure** | | **2,000,000** |
| **RDEC at 20%** | | **400,000** |

Dan Hartley's employment costs (salary, employer's NIC and employer pension contributions) are about £120,000 a year; 60% of his time goes on Ashlar, so £72,000 qualifies. Calder subcontracted part of the sensor design to Brackenwell Sensors Ltd, an invented start-up, for £400,000. Brackenwell was unconnected throughout Calder's AP (Tarnmoor bought it on 1 July GY2, after the AP ended), so 65% qualifies. Had Calder paid Brackenwell after 1 July GY2, the two would have been connected and the connected-party measure, by reference to Brackenwell's own relevant costs, would have applied instead.

The categories are also a test of judgement. A cost is either in a category or out. The adviser's job is to resist stretching a category to cover something that feels like research but is not, and to make sure genuine costs, such as cloud processing of test data, are not left out because nobody told the tax team they existed.

**Payment condition.** Every category has one: nothing can be claimed until it has been paid (CIRD132000).

**What is out.** Repairs to the test bay (the N25 Q1 examiners criticised candidates who included repairs); rent, rates and general overheads; **capital expenditure** (Calder's £500,000 test rig gets an R&D allowance instead: below); overseas contractor costs outside s 1138A.

---

## Who claims, and research done abroad.

**Contracted-out R&D.** Under the merged scheme the company that **decides to undertake or initiate** the R&D claims it (CIRD161000). A contractor cannot claim for R&D contracted to it where the customer intended or contemplated the R&D when the contract was made. So Calder claims 65% of what it paid Brackenwell for the Ashlar sensor design, and Brackenwell cannot claim for that work. This ends the old problem of both parties claiming the same project under different schemes.

**The overseas restriction (CTA 2009 s 1138A).** For APs beginning on or after 1 April 2024, contractor payments for R&D undertaken **outside the UK**, and EPW costs for workers not subject to UK PAYE and NIC, are excluded from **both** schemes unless:

1. conditions necessary for the R&D (geographical, environmental, social, legal or regulatory) are **not present in the UK**;
2. they **are present** where the R&D is undertaken; and
3. it would be **wholly unreasonable** to replicate them in the UK.

The **cost and availability of workers are disregarded** (s 1138A). The unconnected-contractor 65% applies only to the UK (or qualifying overseas) portion: HMRC's draft guidance illustrates a contractor with half its R&D in the UK giving 50% × 65% = **32.5%** of the payment.

*For example*, a payment of £200,000 to an unconnected contractor that performs half of the work in the UK and half abroad (with no s 1138A exception) gives qualifying expenditure of 50% × 65% × £200,000 = **£65,000**.

*For this example only*, suppose Calder paid a laboratory in Vallaria (an invented country) to run the pressure tests because it was cheaper: excluded, because cheaper labour is exactly what the law disregards. If the tests needed a natural geological condition found only in Vallaria, the exception might apply. M25 Q2 tested overseas subcontracting.

**FA 2026 s 34.** Northern Ireland companies claiming ERIS may escape the overseas restriction (a Windsor Framework relaxation, alongside the de minimis State aid limit in s 1112J). FA 2026 s 34 amends s 1138A(1)(b) to begin "for the purposes of relief under Chapter 2", confirming that the relaxation is **ERIS-only**, with effect for claims made on or after **30 October 2024** (retrospective).

---

## Seven steps to cash.

The credit is not simply paid out. It flows through seven steps (CTA 2009 ss 1042I ff; CIRD112100). Picture a waterfall: the credit first fills the company's own tax pool, loses a notional-tax splash, meets a weir set by payroll taxes, and only then flows to other periods, group companies, other taxes and finally the bank.

**Before step 1:** any step 2 amount brought forward from an earlier AP discharges the current AP's CT.

| Step | What happens | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Discharge the company's CT liability for the AP of the claim | Calder stops here: £400,000 < £750,000 |
| 2 | **Notional tax deduction** on any amount left | Rate: **25%** if profits are chargeable at the main rate (**including marginal relief companies**); otherwise **19%** (small profits and loss-making companies). The deducted "step 2 amount" is **not lost**: it may be **surrendered** to a group member or **carried forward** to discharge the company's CT of later periods (s 1042L(3)) |
| 3 | **PAYE cap** | Payable amount limited to **£20,000 + 300%** of the company's relevant PAYE and NIC liabilities for the AP (s 1112B(2); CIRD140000); excess carried forward as credit of the next AP. **Exempt** (HMRC guidance) where the company's staff create or manage IP that it can exploit and connected-party EPW and subcontractor spend is no more than **15%** of qualifying expenditure |
| 4 | Discharge CT of any other AP | |
| 5 | **Surrender** to another group member | Used by the recipient to discharge its CT |
| 6 | Discharge other liabilities to HMRC (VAT, PAYE, contract settlements) | |
| 7 | **Payment** | Conditions apply (for example the company must be a going concern, and HMRC need not pay while the return is under enquiry: s 1112H as summarised in CIRD112100) |

**Step by step, in words.** Step 1 uses the credit against the company's own CT for the period of the claim. Calder stops here, because its £400,000 credit is less than its £750,000 liability. Only if something is left does step 2 apply: the remainder is reduced by notional tax at 25% (main rate profits, including marginal relief companies) or 19% (everyone else, including loss makers). The lower rate for loss makers is the main design concession in the merged scheme (CIRD112100). Step 3 is the payroll weir: cash cannot exceed £20,000 plus three times the company's relevant PAYE and NIC, which targets shell companies with no real payroll, where much of the fraud sat. Anything above the cap is not lost but carried forward as credit of the next AP. Steps 4 to 6 use what remains against the company's CT for other periods, then surrender it to group members, then set it against other HMRC liabilities. Only at step 7 is cash paid.

> **Worked example 10.5: all seven steps (labelled hypothetical, not part of the Tarnmoor story)**
>
> *Suppose* a standalone UK trading company with no associated companies and no group has qualifying expenditure of £1,500,000, adjusted trading profit before RDEC of £100,000, and relevant PAYE and NIC of £40,000. The PAYE cap exemption does not apply.
>
> | | £ |
> |---|---:|
> | RDEC: 20% × £1,500,000 | 300,000 |
> | TTP: £100,000 + £300,000 | 400,000 |
> | CT at 25% (TTP above £250,000) | 100,000 |
> | Step 1: discharge CT of the AP | (100,000) |
> | Remaining | 200,000 |
> | Step 2: notional tax at 25% (profits chargeable at the main rate) = step 2 amount, carried forward against future CT | (50,000) |
> | Remaining | 150,000 |
> | Step 3: PAYE cap £20,000 + 300% × £40,000 = £140,000; excess carried forward as credit of the next AP | (10,000) |
> | Steps 4 to 6: no other CT, no group, no other liabilities | — |
> | **Step 7: payable** | **140,000** |
>
> Had TTP fallen in the marginal relief band (£50,001 to £250,000 with no associates), step 2 would still use **25%**: marginal relief companies are "chargeable at the main rate" for this purpose (CIRD112100).

**Why notional tax?** The credit is taxable. A loss maker pays no tax on it this year, but the credit reduces its loss and so its future relief. Step 2 stops it taking cash today for the tax element.

**Mnemonic:** own tax, notional tax, payroll cap, other periods, group, other taxes, cash.

> **Exam lens: RDEC (grade 1 core)**
> - **Past appearances:** M24 Q4 (10 marks: linked enterprises and the RDEC steps; "poor"; candidates confused step 1, the CT set-off, with step 2, the net value restriction); M25 Q2 (merged scheme inside a CT computation with overseas subcontracting and cloud/software costs; marked leniently because of the rule change); N25 Q1 (merged scheme inside a full computation; repairs wrongly included).
> - **Style:** usually embedded in a 15–20 mark computation; "Calculate, with explanations". 0.5–1 mark per point: the credit as a trading receipt, the 20% rate, each excluded cost, the step 1 set-off, the step 2 rate with its reason.
> - **Traps:** treating RDEC as a deduction rather than a taxable credit; 25% versus 19% notional tax (marginal relief companies use 25%); including capital items, repairs or overseas contractor costs; 65% for unconnected contractors and EPWs; forgetting claim notification for a first claim.
> - **Layout:** add the RDEC in the CT pro forma as trading income; deduct it from the CT liability below the line; show steps in order.

## Surrender inside the group.

Step 5 is where a large group finds value. A loss-making subsidiary can take cash, net of notional tax and subject to the PAYE cap; or it can surrender the credit to a taxpaying group company, which uses it to pay its own CT. Inside a group with a large tax bill, surrender turns a deferred, restricted asset into an immediate saving, and the step 2 amount, which would otherwise sit idle in a company that will make losses for years, can travel too.

*In our invented case*, Tom Hesketh, the group head of tax, compares the options for Brackenwell's GY2 credit. Cash would bring in £486,000 now, with the £114,000 step 2 amount carried forward against tax Brackenwell may not pay for years. Surrender to Tarnmoor Engineering, whose GY2 CT is £2,226,250, uses the whole £600,000 at once. He surrenders both amounts. The surrendered credit discharges TEL's liability when Brackenwell's claim is made; TEL's instalments are still based on its full liability (our reading of HMRC's guidance at CIRD89870, which deals with a company's own credit).

> **Worked example 10.2: Brackenwell's merged credit, GY2 (year to 31 December GY2) (invented)**
>
> Tarnmoor plc buys Brackenwell Sensors Ltd (BSL) on **1 July GY2**. Its founder Dr Asha Varma stays as CTO. BSL is linked to Tarnmoor at the end of GY2, so (HMRC's view: next section) it is large for the **whole** year and claims the merged RDEC on qualifying expenditure of **£3,000,000**.
>
> | Step | £ |
> |---|---:|
> | RDEC: 20% × £3,000,000 | 600,000 |
> | Step 1: BSL's own CT for GY2 (loss-making) | nil |
> | Step 2: notional tax at **19%** (loss maker) | (114,000) |
> | Remaining after step 2 | **486,000** |
> | Step 3: PAYE cap £20,000 + 300% × £900,000 relevant PAYE/NIC = £2,720,000: not restrictive | — |
> | Step 4: no other CT liabilities | — |
> | Step 5: surrendered to Tarnmoor Engineering Ltd (TEL) | (486,000) |
> | Step 2 amount also surrendered to TEL (s 1042L) | 114,000 |
> | **Total credit discharging TEL's GY2 CT of £2,226,250** | **600,000** |
>
> **Group economics:** the credit is taxable in BSL, so BSL's GY2 loss is £600,000 smaller. The loss is time-apportioned, so half of that reduction (£300,000) falls on the post-acquisition loss surrendered to TEL and half on the pre-acquisition loss, which is restricted (chapter 14). Valuing the whole reduction at 25% gives a cost of £150,000 and a net benefit of **£450,000** = 15% of £3,000,000; because the pre-acquisition half may never be usable, the near-term cost is lower. The steps move cash; the rate decides value.
>
> **Payment for the surrender.** TEL pays BSL £600,000 under a written agreement. Under **CTA 2009 s 1042N(5)–(6)** (inserted by **FA 2026 s 31**, for payments made on or after **26 November 2025**), a payment for surrendered RDEC that does not exceed the credit surrendered is **ignored** in computing both companies' profits and is **not a distribution**. Any excess is outside the protection.

## Research and development intensive companies.

ERIS (enhanced R&D intensive support, CTA 2009 Part 13 Ch 2) is for one kind of company only: a **loss-making R&D-intensive SME**.

**Size (CIRD91400–92000).** The R&D SME definition in CTA 2009 Part 13 is the European Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC with the ceilings **doubled**:

| Test | Recommendation ceiling | R&D relief ceiling |
|---|---|---|
| Staff headcount | under 250 | **under 500** |
| Turnover | €50m | **€100m** |
| Balance sheet total | €43m | **€86m** |

Staff **and** either the turnover or the balance sheet test. **Linked enterprises** (broadly control, usually more than 50% of voting rights) are aggregated **in full**; **partner enterprises** (broadly 25% to 50%) are aggregated **in proportion** (CIRD91500, CIRD91700). Sterling figures are converted to euros at the balance sheet date rate. The 2026 CTA tax tables reproduce the SME definition, including notes for R&D (check the 2027 tables).

**Intensity.** Relevant R&D expenditure at least **30%** of total relevant expenditure, with connected companies' figures aggregated; **one year's grace** if the test was met in the previous 12-month AP with a valid claim.

**The relief.**
- Extra deduction **86%** of qualifying expenditure (186% in total).
- **Surrenderable loss** = the lower of the **unrelieved trading loss** (after current-period sideways relief and group relief; losses brought forward or carried back ignored) and **186% of the related qualifying expenditure** (CIRD122000).
- Payable credit **14.5%** of the loss surrendered; **not taxable**; the loss surrendered is extinguished.
- Maximum value 186% × 14.5% = **26.97%** of qualifying expenditure in cash.
- The **PAYE cap** and its exemption apply. NI companies: extra relief limited to de minimis State aid (s 1112J, substituted by FA 2025 s 29).

The two reliefs differ in kind, not just in rate. RDEC is a taxable credit that any trading company can use. ERIS is an enhanced deduction that creates or increases a loss, part of which can then be swapped for a non-taxable cash credit. A company that surrenders its loss for ERIS cash gives up that loss for carry-forward or group relief; a company with taxable profits gets the extra deduction but no cash. ERIS is therefore aimed at one profile: the young, cash-hungry, loss-making developer whose research is most of what it does, which is exactly what Brackenwell was before the acquisition.

> **Worked example 10.3: Brackenwell before acquisition (year to 31 December GY1) (invented)**
>
> BSL: independent; 45 staff; owned by its founders and venture investors (no partner or linked enterprise on the invented facts).
>
> | | £ |
> |---|---:|
> | Intensity: £3,500,000 ÷ £5,000,000 | **70%** (≥ 30%) |
> | Trading loss before enhancement (after deducting £3,500,000 qualifying expenditure) | (4,200,000) |
> | Extra deduction: 86% × £3,500,000 | (3,010,000) |
> | **Trading loss after enhancement** | **(7,210,000)** |
> | Cap: 186% × £3,500,000 | 6,510,000 |
> | Unrelieved loss (no other profits, no group) | 7,210,000 |
> | **Surrenderable loss (lower)** | **6,510,000** |
> | **Payable credit: 14.5% × £6,510,000** | **943,950** |
> | PAYE cap: £20,000 + 300% × £900,000 = £2,720,000: not restrictive | — |
> | **Loss carried forward** (£7,210,000 − £6,510,000) | **700,000** |
>
> Effective rate £943,950 ÷ £3,500,000 = 26.97%. The pending credit is a deal point: the SPA should say whether the price includes it and who bears any HMRC reduction (chapter 20).

## Linked enterprises and the cliff edge of acquisition.

**The misconception:** "a subsidiary of a large group can claim the SME-style intensive relief if it is small itself". It cannot. Size is tested across **linked enterprises**. The moment Tarnmoor owns BSL, the group's staff (about 6,000) and revenue (over £1bn) are added to BSL's: BSL is no longer an SME and can claim only the merged RDEC. M24 Q4 turned on exactly this (a parent and its R&D subsidiary were linked; most candidates missed it).

**Timing (HMRC's view).** The Recommendation normally lets a company keep its status until it crosses the thresholds in **two consecutive** years. **HMRC's view** (CIRD92000) is that the cushion does not apply on a **takeover** by a large group: the company is treated as **large for the whole AP** in which it is acquired, including the months before completion. Hence BSL's GY2 claim is a merged RDEC claim on all £3.0m, including January to June.

This is HMRC guidance, not statute, but it is how claims are processed. Advisers sometimes suggest ending the target's AP at completion so that the pre-acquisition months form a separate AP that can still be tested as an SME. *In our invented case*, nobody thought of it in time: put R&D status on the due diligence list before signing.

**Partner enterprises in reverse.** A small company part-owned (25%–50%) by an investor must include a proportion of the investor's figures. The Recommendation has special rules for some investor types (for example certain venture capital investors); check them in CIRD92800 (text of the Recommendation) on real facts. *In our invented case* BSL's venture investors did not make it a partner or linked enterprise of any larger group.

> **Going further: R&D in the Brackenwell deal (invented)**
> - **Pending credit.** BSL's GY1 ERIS credit of £943,950 related to a period when it was independent. If the claim is made after completion, the cash arrives in a Tarnmoor company; the SPA should say whether the price already reflects it, and who bears the loss if HMRC enquires into the claim and reduces it (an indemnity or a price adjustment: chapter 20).
> - **Status of the acquisition year.** On HMRC's whole-period view, BSL's January to June GY2 spending gets the merged RDEC, not ERIS. Ending BSL's AP on 30 June GY2 was the planning point that was missed.
> - **Payment step 7 conditions.** A target that is not a going concern, or has PAYE or VAT arrears, may find its cash credit delayed; due diligence should check both.
> - **Losses.** The ERIS credit extinguishes the losses surrendered, and the remaining £0.7m joins BSL's other pre-acquisition losses, which chapter 14 shows are restricted after the change in ownership.
> - **Claim history.** HMRC enquiries into past R&D claims are common; a target with aggressive historic claims (or contingent-fee advisers) is a warranty and indemnity issue.

> **Exam lens: ERIS and linked enterprises (grade 1 core in 2026; not examined from 2028)**
> - **Past appearances:** M24 Q4 (linked enterprises; poor).
> - **Traps:** testing the subsidiary alone; forgetting partner enterprises; using the transfer pricing SME thresholds (250 staff, €50m/€43m) instead of the doubled R&D ceilings (500, €100m/€86m); applying 14.5% to the whole enhanced loss rather than the lower of the unrelieved loss and 186% of qualifying expenditure; treating the ERIS credit as taxable.
> - **2028:** the reformed syllabus drops R&D-intensive SMEs from LCG; this does not affect the 2027 sittings.

---

## Telling HMRC first.

Back to Graham Pike and his clock. Two procedural requirements now guard every claim, and both were responses to the error and fraud figures.

**Claim notification (CTA 2009 s 1142A).** For APs beginning on or after 1 April 2023, a company must notify HMRC in advance if:
- it is claiming for the **first time**; or
- it has not made a claim in the **3 years ending with the last day of the claim notification period** (also where HMRC removed an earlier claim, and ignoring amendment-claims for pre-April 2023 APs made on or after 1 April 2023).

The **claim notification period** runs from the **first day of the period of account** to **6 months after the end of the period of account** (GOV.UK guidance). Without a notification, a claim made after that period ends is **invalid**. Content: SI 2023/813 (Content of Claim Notifications, Additional Information Requirements and Miscellaneous Amendments) Regulations; delivered electronically under HMRC's directions, naming the company officer responsible.

| Company | Period of account | Previous claim in 3 years? | Notification deadline |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calder | 1 April GY1 – 31 March GY2 | No (never claimed: invented assumption) | **30 September GY2** (filed April GY2) |
| BSL | Year to 31 December GY2 | Yes (ERIS for GY1) | Not required |

**Traps.** The window runs from the **period of account**, not the accounting period: where a long period of account is split into two APs, the six months run from the end of the period of account. A company whose last claim was over three years ago is a first-time claimant again.

**Additional information form (FA 1998 Sch 18 para 83EA).** Mandatory for claims made on or after **8 August 2023**, submitted **before** the claim in the return, giving projects, costs by category and people involved. HMRC may **remove** a claim made without complying with a requirement (para 83EB).

**Time limit (FA 1998 Sch 18 para 83E).** A claim may be made, amended or withdrawn within **2 years** from the end of the period of account (periods up to 18 months; 42 months from the start for longer periods). HMRC has a discretion to accept late claims (para 83E(5); SP 5/01).

> **Going further: the group R&D calendar**
> Tom Hesketh's team keeps a register of every company doing R&D: period of account, last claim date, notification deadline, AIF status, return date. Joiners, newly formed subsidiaries and companies that pause R&D are the usual casualties. A missed notification is not a technicality HMRC can overlook: the law says the claim cannot be made.
