# Part Four: Across Borders.

# Chapter 22: Where a company lives, and how it leaves.

On 1 March GY4 a letter left Leeds for HMRC. It came from Tarnmoor Ireland Ltd (TIL), a company in our invented group, Tarnmoor. Tarnmoor, its companies, its people and its numbers are invented for teaching, as they are throughout this book. Ireland is real. The letter said three things. TIL intended to stop being resident in the UK. It would do so at the end of 30 June. And here was a statement of the tax it owed, with a proposal for how that tax would be secured before it went.

TIL was incorporated in Ireland. Its customers were Irish. Yet for years it had paid UK corporation tax on every euro it earned, because its directors met in Leeds. Now the board had decided to move its meetings, and its real decisions, to Dublin. A company cannot simply walk out of the UK tax net. It must tell HMRC first, account for what it owes, and pay tax on gains it has never realised.

This chapter asks two questions. Where does a company live for tax purposes? And what happens when it leaves? It opens Part Four, on profits that cross borders. On the LCG grid, **company residence** (with the chargeable profits of non-UK resident companies) and **non-resident and dual resident companies** (gains) are **core (grade 1)**; **migration of a company (post 1 January 2020 only)** is **non-core (grade 2)**. The chapter builds on *The Living Law* (TKS), chapter 20 (company residence and *De Beers*) and chapter 26 (the treaty tie-breaker, including Article 4 of the Multilateral Instrument for the UK and Ireland). Here we take both to Advanced Technical depth, then follow TIL out of the door.

| Statute | Short name used | What it holds here |
|---|---|---|
| Corporation Tax Act 2009 (CTA 2009) | the 2009 Act | ss 14, 18 (residence); s 10 (AP ends); ss 41, 162 (deemed cessation, stock); s 333 (loan relationships); s 609 (derivatives); s 859 (intangibles) |
| Corporation Tax Act 2010 (CTA 2010) | the 2010 Act | s 109 (dual resident investing companies and group relief) |
| Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA 1992) | the Gains Act | s 185 (exit charge); s 187 (repealed); s 187B (UK land); ss 171, 175 (DRICs) |
| Capital Allowances Act 2001 (CAA 2001) | the Capital Allowances Act | s 577(2), s 61(1)(f) (discontinuance and balancing adjustments); ss 266, 570 (DRICs) |
| Taxes Management Act 1970 (TMA 1970) | the Management Act | ss 109B–109F (notice, security, penalties, recovery); Sch 3ZB (exit charge payment plans) |

We apply the law for FY2026. FA 2026 made no change to company residence or the migration rules (no residence consultation was found for 2023–2026 either).

---

## Two tests, one question.

Residence decides how much of a company's income the UK claims. A UK resident company is charged on all its profits wherever they arise, subject to reliefs such as the branch exemption (chapter 25) and foreign tax credit (chapter 24). A non-resident company is charged only on narrow categories of UK profit, such as a trade carried on through a UK permanent establishment or UK property income (CTA 2009 s 5; chapter 23 owns that list). Residence is the first switch in every international answer.

There are two tests, and a company need pass only one.

1. **Incorporation (statute).** A company incorporated in the UK is UK resident (CTA 2009 s 14). It does not matter where its directors live, where its board meets or where it trades: a company registered at Companies House carries its residence with it like a birth certificate.
2. **Central management and control (case law).** A company incorporated abroad is UK resident if its central management and control (CMC) is exercised here. The House of Lords settled the test in *De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd v Howe* [1906] AC 455, where a South African-registered diamond company with South African mines was UK resident because the directors who made its real decisions met in London (TKS chapter 20).

The two tests work as a ratchet. Incorporation keeps a UK company resident whatever happens to its board. CMC can make a foreign company resident too, and a foreign company can drift in and out of residence as its decision making moves. Only one route takes residence away from a UK-incorporated company, and it runs through a treaty (s 18, below).

> **Misconception: "a UK company can move its tax residence abroad by moving its board."** It cannot. Moving the board of a UK-incorporated company leaves it UK resident under s 14. At most it becomes dual resident. Whether it then becomes non-resident depends on a treaty tie-breaker (and, under the Multilateral Instrument, on the two tax authorities agreeing): CTA 2009 s 18. A board meeting in Paris does not change a birth certificate issued by Companies House.

TIL shows the other side of the ratchet. It was incorporated in Ireland, so s 14 never applied to it. It was UK resident only because its CMC was in Leeds. Move the control to Dublin, genuinely and completely, and it stops being UK resident as a matter of domestic law.

---

## Where the mind of a company lives.

CMC sounds precise and is not. The courts have always treated it as a question of fact. In *De Beers*, Lord Loreburn LC said that "the real business is carried on where the central management and control actually abides" (at 458, as quoted in *Wood v Holden*).

Think of a company as having a body and a mind. The body is its factories, offices, staff and customers; the mind is the small group of people who decide its strategy, approve major contracts, raise finance, declare dividends and appoint managers. Residence follows the mind. The test looks for the **highest level of control**, not day-to-day management: the factory manager in Cork who runs production is managing; the board in Leeds that decides whether to build the factory, how to fund it and whether to sell it is exercising CMC.

In most companies the highest level of control is exercised by the board, acting as a board. So the usual question is where the board meets and decides; but that is a starting point, not an answer. **HMRC's view** is set out in Statement of Practice 1/90, reproduced at INTM120200: the location of board meetings, "although important in the normal case", is not necessarily conclusive; the place of directors' meetings "is significant only insofar as those meetings constitute the medium through which central management and control is exercised".

Two warnings follow. A board which meets abroad but merely signs decisions made elsewhere is not exercising control there: the meeting is theatre. And a board can exercise control without meeting at all, through written resolutions, calls and informal decisions; if the directors who really decide all live and work in the UK, the company may be UK resident even if its formal meetings are held offshore.

HMRC's guidance also recognises modern board practice. It gives examples where it would **not usually review** residence, including a UK-based director who habitually joins overseas meetings by electronic link (INTM120150), and its pandemic guidance accepts that a company does not necessarily become UK resident because a few board meetings are held, or some decisions taken, here for a short period (INTM120185). These are statements of HMRC practice, not law: they say where HMRC will look, not what a court would find.

**In our invented case,** before GY4 TIL was UK resident on the plainest facts. Its board was made up of Tarnmoor executives based in Leeds; it met in Leeds; it approved the Irish budgets, the purchase of a UK warehouse (GY1) and the acquisition of an Irish distributor's business (GY2). Its residence was no accident: it kept TIL inside the UK group for group relief and the gains rules (chapter 1).

---

## Usurped, or merely influenced.

Most foreign subsidiaries of UK groups have boards abroad that listen closely to the parent. The cases that matter most to a group tax function ask: when a parent tells a subsidiary's board what it wants, where is the subsidiary's mind?

**Usurped.** In *Unit Construction Co Ltd v Bullock* [1960] AC 351 (HL), a UK company's African subsidiaries had constitutions requiring their boards to meet, and their business to be managed, outside the UK. In practice the local boards stood back and the parent's board in London took the real decisions. The subsidiaries were UK resident. Lord Radcliffe treated the location of control as a matter of fact, of "actuality"; it did not matter that the parent's conduct was contrary to the subsidiaries' constitutions. Residence follows what happens, not what the documents say should happen.

**Influenced.** *Wood v Holden* [2006] EWCA Civ 26 (Chadwick LJ giving the leading judgment; Moore-Bick LJ and Sir Christopher Staughton). Note first: Mr Wood was the businessman behind Ron Wood Greetings Card Holdings Ltd, **not the musician**. In July 1996 the shares, held through an offshore company in the Woods' structure (Copsewood Investments Ltd, a British Virgin Islands company), were sold for £23.7m to a Dutch company, Eulalia Holding BV, whose sole managing director was a Dutch trust company; three months later Eulalia sold them on to a trade buyer for about £30.8m. Mr and Mrs Wood were assessed on the gains under TCGA 1992 s 13 (gains of non-resident close companies), and the planning depended on Eulalia being resident outside the UK. HMRC argued that Eulalia's director simply did what Mr Wood and his advisers wanted, so no real decisions were taken in the Netherlands. The Special Commissioners agreed; Park J reversed them; the Court of Appeal upheld Park J. Eulalia was Dutch resident.

The distinction is the one every group tax function lives by:

| Board that is... | Result | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Bypassed: stands aside while someone else decides | Usurped: the company lives where the usurper decides | *Unit Construction* |
| Advised, proposed to and influenced, but itself considers and takes the decision | Keeps CMC | *Wood v Holden* |
| Formally decides, but implements an uncommercial decision really taken by the parent | Parent's location | *Development Securities* (below) |

A client who always follows a solicitor's advice still makes the decision; only a client who hands over the pen has stopped deciding. The legal rule is narrower: the court asks whether the board actually considered and took the decisions that matter, at the highest level of the company's affairs, and where. Influence is not control. But *Wood v Holden* is reassuring only up to a point: a board that never asks a question will not necessarily be respected.

---

## When the parent really decides.

*HMRC v Development Securities plc* [2020] EWCA Civ 1705 (David Richards, Newey and Nugee LJJ) is the modern counterweight. Development Securities, a UK property group, used a 2004 scheme devised by a large accountancy firm to make use of indexation allowance on assets standing at a loss. New Jersey subsidiaries with Jersey-resident directors were to buy assets from the group under options at prices well above market value, and later become UK resident. The scheme depended on their being Jersey resident when they bought.

| Tribunal | Finding |
|---|---|
| FTT | Jersey boards had not acted improperly and had checked legality, but had not engaged with the uncommercial substance; they implemented the parent's decision: **UK resident** |
| UT | The directors had applied their minds and had not abdicated their responsibilities: **Jersey resident** |
| Court of Appeal | UT's criticisms of the FTT not well-founded; FTT decision restored: **UK resident** when the options were exercised |

The case did not overrule *Wood v Holden*. Both ask by whom, and where, the real decision was taken; the answers differed on the facts. Eulalia's director took a decision that was, for Eulalia, an ordinary one. The Jersey directors approved transactions against their own companies' interests that made sense only for the group. A board that signs something uncommercial for its own company because the parent wants it is hard to describe as the company's mind.

The reasoning was not unanimous: one member of the court expressed "very considerable reservations" about the FTT's reasoning while agreeing with the outcome, and commentators still debate how much active engagement is enough. Two lessons are clear: a subsidiary board asked to do something uncommercial will be scrutinised hard; and evidence that the board understood, questioned and could have refused a proposal is far more persuasive than evidence that it met in the right place.

**In our invented case,** TIL's migration turned the lesson around. To leave the UK, its control had to move to Dublin in fact, not just on paper. The board was reconstituted with effect from the end of 30 June GY4: a majority of Irish-resident directors with industry experience joined, the Leeds executives stepped down, and meetings moved to Dublin. The board was given authority over budgets, contracts and financing, and used it. Tom Hesketh, the group head of tax, wrote the new governance protocol; its first line read (in our invented story) "decisions are made in the room, not before it".

> **Going further: governance for overseas subsidiaries.** The same lesson runs the other way for subsidiaries a group wants to keep abroad (for Tarnmoor, TVS in Vallaria and TCM in Marrovia, both invented). A defensible file shows: directors resident locally with the skills to decide; board packs circulated in time to be read; minutes that record discussion, questions and alternatives, not just resolutions; decisions taken at the meeting, not pre-agreed by e-mail from the parent; a delegation framework that lets the local board say no; and an annual residence review by the tax function. The group may propose and influence (*Wood v Holden*); it must not decide for them (*Unit Construction*, *Development Securities*). A subsidiary properly resident abroad still meets the CFC rules (chapter 26).

---

## Two countries, one company.

Residence tests are national, and nothing stops two countries claiming the same company. A company incorporated in one country and managed in another will often be resident in both: dual residence.

Treaties solve the problem in two steps (TKS chapter 26):

1. **Treaty residence.** Article 4(1) of a treaty based on the OECD Model treats as resident a person "liable to tax therein by reason of their domicile, residence, place of management or other criterion of a similar nature", excluding persons liable only on local-source income (HMRC's description, INTM153050).
2. **Tie-breaker** for a person resident in both:
   - **Older treaties:** resident only where its **place of effective management** (POEM) is situated. POEM is a treaty concept, not the same words as CMC, though on most facts the two point to the same place. HMRC: "Typically the tie-breaker awards residence to the country in which the effective management of the company is located" (INTM154050).
   - **MLI Article 4** (the Multilateral Instrument, in force for the UK from 1 October 2018): the competent authorities "shall endeavour to determine by mutual agreement" the company's residence, having regard to its place of effective management, place of incorporation and other relevant factors; without agreement, no treaty relief except as the authorities agree. The UK and Ireland both adopted it; for UK corporation tax it has effect from **1 April 2020** (HMRC's synthesised UK–Ireland text).

**Treaty non-residence in domestic law.** CTA 2009 s 18: a company that would be UK resident but is regarded by a treaty as resident only in the other territory is treated as **not UK resident for all purposes of the Taxes Acts** (from 30 November 1993; formerly FA 1994 s 249). It is the only route by which a UK-incorporated company can become non-resident, and under MLI Article 4 it now depends on an agreement between tax authorities, not on a rule a company can engineer by moving its meetings.

**Timing.** *HMRC v Smallwood* [2010] EWCA Civ 778 concerned a marketed "round the world" trust scheme: UK trustees were replaced by a Mauritian trustee, a gain was realised, and UK trustees were reappointed within the same tax year. The majority held that the tie-breaker could not be applied as a "snapshot" at the moment of disposal; viewed in the context of the whole scheme, POEM was in the UK and the UK could tax. Smallwood involved trustees, not a company, but the lesson carries over: a tie-breaker is not a stopwatch to be started and stopped around a transaction.

> **Exam lens: residence and dual residence.**
> - **Grade:** company residence and chargeable profits of non-UK resident companies **1 (core)**; non-resident and dual resident companies (gains) **1 (core)**. Check the 2027 grid when published (no change expected: the 2028 grid keeps residence in the key principles).
> - **Past appearances:** **N23 Q1** (20 marks, 9/3/8): residence of an Anglo-Belgian parent before and after board changes (incorporation, CMC, **supplied treaty tie-breaker** using POEM), CT administration and a CFC finance company; generally good, but some candidates used the OECD Model instead of the **supplied article**, and some strayed into DPT and CIR. **N24 Q6** (10 marks): a non-UK company setting up in the UK by branch or subsidiary: PE, CMC, UK residence, when a non-resident is chargeable; very well answered when tied to the scenario.
> - **Style:** technical prose; apply each test in turn (incorporation, CMC, treaty, s 18) to the facts at each date; 0.5–1 mark per point.
> - **Traps:** saying a UK company becomes non-resident by moving its board; using the Model's wording when an extract is supplied; treating board location as conclusive; forgetting s 18 makes treaty non-residence apply for **all** tax purposes.

**In our invented case,** TIL was dual resident before migrating: UK resident by CMC in Leeds; Ireland also treated it as resident; and the two competent authorities had agreed, before the story begins, that it was UK resident for treaty purposes. (This book does not discuss Irish domestic law.) When control moved to Dublin, TIL ceased to be UK resident under domestic law, and the authorities agreed it was Irish resident from the migration date.

---

## What dual residence costs.

A company that stays UK resident while also resident abroad (because the tie-breaker favours the UK, or no treaty applies) is inside the UK charge, but Parliament is wary of it: a company taxed in two countries can sometimes deduct one expense in both, or use one loss twice. The rules target the **dual resident investing company** (DRIC), broadly a dual resident company that is not a trading company, or whose trade consists mainly of holding shares, making loans or similar group-finance activities.

| Rule | Effect | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Group relief | A dual resident company cannot surrender losses if it meets the DRIC conditions | CTA 2010 s 109 |
| No gain, no loss | A DRIC cannot receive assets at no gain, no loss within a gains group | TCGA 1992 s 171(2)(d) |
| Group roll-over | Excluded where a DRIC would apply the proceeds | TCGA 1992 s 175(2) |
| Capital allowances | Connected-party succession elections (transfer at TWDV) and s 570 elections barred where a DRIC is involved | CAA 2001 s 266(1)(c), s 570(2)(b) |
| Branch exemption | While dual resident, a company cannot exempt PE profits in the territory in which it is treaty resident (HMRC's view) | INTM287010; chapter 25 |

The examiners tested the DRIC group relief bar in **N24 Q2** (20 marks, group and consortium relief), and reported that it was missed.

**In our invented case,** TIL escaped all of this. It was a trading company (distributing valves and parts), so not a DRIC. While UK resident it could surrender and claim group relief (chapter 1) and receive assets at no gain, no loss. Its dual residence was a fact to manage: the tax function kept the competent authority agreement on file, reviewed board minutes each year, and made sure no Irish meeting quietly took a decision that belonged in Leeds.

**SAO.** The senior accounting officer rules turn on UK incorporation. TIL (Irish-incorporated) was never inside them, even while UK resident; its migration changes nothing on that front (chapter 4).

---

## Leaving, and why leaving costs money.

When a company stops being UK resident, three things happen at once: its accounting period ends; the UK loses its claim to tax its future foreign profits and gains; and it may carry assets that grew in value while it was resident, untaxed because unrealised.

**The AP ends** (CTA 2009 s 10(1)(g); chapter 3). TIL's AP that began on 1 January GY4 ended on 30 June GY4. Its return for those six months is the migration return, and every exit charge falls into it.

**Why exit charges.** A resident company is taxed on worldwide gains when realised; if it could leave just before selling, gains built up during residence would escape. So departure itself is treated as a realisation. Picture a hotel guest who has been helping themselves from the minibar all week: the hotel presents the bill at checkout, not after the guest has finished the bottles at home. The rule: the company is treated as disposing of its assets at market value immediately before it leaves, and reacquiring them at that value.

**The old group postponement is gone.** TCGA s 187 let a company leaving as a 75% subsidiary of a UK-resident company jointly elect to postpone the gain on its foreign trading assets. It was **repealed by FA 2019 Sch 8 para 9**, where s 185 applies on a company ceasing to be UK resident **on or after 1 January 2020** (para 9(5)). For migrations since then, the gains charge can only be **paid** over time, under a payment plan, where the company qualifies.

**Where today's rules come from.** In *National Grid Indus BV* (C-371/10), decided by the Court of Justice in 2011, a Dutch company moved its place of effective management to the UK and the Netherlands taxed its unrealised gains at once. The Court held that a member state may fix the tax on gains accrued within its jurisdiction, but that immediate recovery was disproportionate; offering deferral, possibly with interest, would be acceptable [secondary sources; the judgment was not opened]. The UK introduced exit charge payment plans (FA 2013 Sch 49, inserting TMA Sch 3ZB) with effect from **11 December 2012** (CG13430). The EU Anti Tax Avoidance Directive then set a common model, and FA 2019 Sch 8 (made while the UK was still bound) turned the plans into fixed instalments over five years. Rules shaped by EU freedoms remain on the UK statute book in EU form: a post-Brexit oddity with a practical consequence (below).

---

## The gains exit charge, and the land that waits.

**TCGA 1992 s 185.** When a company ceases to be UK resident it is deemed to dispose of **all its assets** at market value immediately before the relevant time and to reacquire them at that value (s 185(2); CG42370). Every chargeable asset is caught, wherever situated, unless excepted. Indexation runs only to December 2017 for assets held before then; losses on the deemed disposals are allowable in the ordinary way.

| Rule | Detail | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Excepted assets | Assets situated in the UK and used or held for a trade carried on through a UK PE after migration (they stay within the UK charge: chapter 23) | s 185(4) |
| Roll-over blocked | No roll-over from an asset disposed of before migration into an asset acquired after it, unless the new asset is a UK PE asset | s 185 |
| Ceasing to exist | Is not ceasing to be resident: the charge is about departure, not death | s 185 |
| Old postponement | s 187 repealed for migrations on or after 1 January 2020 | FA 2019 Sch 8 para 9 |

**UK land: s 187B.** Since **6 April 2019** non-resident companies have been chargeable on gains on UK land and certain indirect interests in it (TCGA s 2B, Sch 1A; chapter 23). So there is no need to tax UK land at departure: the UK can tax it when it is sold. **TCGA s 187B** (substituted by FA 2019 Sch 1 para 67): where an interest in UK land is deemed disposed of under s 185(2), the gain or loss **does not accrue at migration**; on a later disposal of the whole or part of the interest, the postponed amount is treated as accruing then, **in addition to** the gain or loss on the actual disposal.

- **Automatic:** no claim.
- **Election out:** the company may elect to exclude a deemed disposal from s 187B **within 2 years** after the day of the deemed disposal (s 187B(5)–(6)). Reasons: a **loss** on the land that the company wants in its migration period against other gains, or capital losses available now to absorb the gain.
- **Two layers on a later sale:** base cost after migration = market value at migration (the s 185 reacquisition), so the actual gain measures post-departure growth and the postponed amount measures pre-departure growth. Together they equal the gain over original cost: nothing lost, nothing taxed twice.

> **Worked example 22.1: TIL's English warehouse (invented)**
>
> TIL bought the warehouse in GY1 for £3,000,000 and let it to an unconnected logistics company. Market value at migration (30 June GY4): £3,800,000.
>
> | £ | |
> |---|---|
> | Deemed proceeds (s 185(2)) | 3,800,000 |
> | Cost | (3,000,000) |
> | Indexation (acquired after December 2017) | nil |
> | Deemed gain | 800,000 |
> | Accruing at migration (s 187B) | **nil** (postponed) |
>
> **Illustration only (not a story fact): suppose TIL later sells the warehouse for £4,500,000.**
>
> | £ | |
> |---|---|
> | Proceeds | 4,500,000 |
> | Base cost (market value at migration) | (3,800,000) |
> | Actual gain | 700,000 |
> | Postponed gain accruing on the same disposal (s 187B) | 800,000 |
> | **Total chargeable** | **1,500,000** |
> | Check: proceeds less original cost (4,500,000 − 3,000,000) | 1,500,000 |
>
> Had TIL elected out within two years, the £800,000 would have been taxed in the migration AP: CT at 25% of **£200,000**, eventually payable either way.

---

## The other exits.

Gains are only one kind of value a departing company carries. Each income code has its own exit, and an AT answer lists them all. **N25 Q3** expected trading stock, machinery, derivatives, land and intangibles.

**The trade: deemed cessation.** When a company ceases to be within the charge to CT in respect of a trade, it is treated as permanently ceasing to carry it on (CTA 2009 s 41(2)). A company that migrates and keeps no UK PE is in exactly that position: its trade carries on in the real world, but for UK tax it has stopped.

| Item | Exit rule | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Trading stock | Valued under the cessation rules: unless sold to a person who carries on (or will carry on) a UK trade and can deduct the cost, brought in at the amount it would have realised on an open-market sale at cessation | CTA 2009 ss 41, 162 |
| Plant and machinery | End of the qualifying activity is a disposal event (CAA s 61(1)(f), applied by s 577(2) where a company ceases to be within the charge, per HMRC OT42550); plant kept is brought in at market value; balancing charge or allowance in the final chargeable period; **no WDA** in that period | CAA 2001 ss 55, 61, 577 |
| Intangible fixed assets | Deemed realisation and reacquisition at **market value** immediately before ceasing to be resident; credit = MV − TWDV | CTA 2009 s 859 |
| Loan relationships | Deemed assignment and reacquisition at **fair value** immediately before ceasing to be resident; excludes items held for a UK PE, a UK land dealing or development trade, a UK property business or other UK property income | CTA 2009 s 333 |
| Derivative contracts | As loan relationships, at fair value | CTA 2009 s 609 |
| Chargeable assets (including shares) | s 185 deemed disposal; for shares, test the SSE first (chapter 18): at least 10% needed | TCGA 1992 s 185; Sch 7AC |

> **Trap (N25 Q3).** The derivatives exit (s 609) is a fair value measurement on departure. It has nothing to do with the Disregard Regulations (chapter 12); the examiners reported that some candidates wrongly discussed them.

The pattern is simple. Every exit turns value accrued under UK jurisdiction into taxable profit, at market or fair value, on the last day of residence. A good answer walks through the balance sheet asset by asset, asking which code taxes each one and whether an exception keeps it in the UK.

> **Exam lens: migration exits.**
> - **Grade:** migration of company (post 1 January 2020 only) **2 (non-core)**: working knowledge plus the main computation. The gains exit (s 185) also sits within "non-resident and dual resident companies" **1 (core)**.
> - **Past appearance:** **N25 Q3** (15 marks): residence tests; exit charges on deemed disposal, trading stock, machinery, derivatives, land and intangibles; **UK land automatically postponed** (the land in the question had been acquired after 5 April 2019); payment plans; notice and statement to HMRC and penalties. Common errors: **missing the automatic land postponement**, wrongly discussing the Disregard Regulations, and weak administration and payment plan detail.
> - **Layout:** a schedule of assets (book value, market value, exit amount, code, plan-eligible?), then the CT for the migration AP, then CT1 − CT2.
> - **Traps:** citing s 187 postponement (repealed); taxing UK land at migration; forgetting stock and plant (the deemed cessation); forgetting that the AP ends on migration; offering a payment plan to a UK-incorporated company.

---

## Tarnmoor Ireland's last six months.

> **Worked example 22.2: TIL's migration AP, 1 January – 30 June GY4 (invented)**
>
> Ordinary trading profit for the six months: £1,200,000. (The warehouse's net rental profit for the six months is ignored for simplicity.) TIL owed TPLC £20m, interest free and repayable on demand: a loan repayable on demand is worth its face value, so s 333 gives no credit or debit. TIL had no derivatives.
>
> **Exit schedule (immediately before the end of 30 June GY4)**
>
> | Asset | Book / tax value £ | Market value £ | Exit amount £ | Rule | In CT1 − CT2? |
> |---|---|---|---|---|---|
> | Trading stock | 1,100,000 | 1,400,000 | 300,000 | CTA 2009 ss 41, 162 | Yes |
> | Customer list (bought GY2; no debits, s 879I; TWDV = cost) | 3,000,000 | 4,200,000 | 1,200,000 | CTA 2009 s 859 | Yes |
> | 8% of an unconnected Irish distributor (bought GY1; no SSE; no indexation) | 900,000 | 1,500,000 | 600,000 | TCGA s 185 | Yes |
> | Plant and machinery pool | 400,000 | 500,000 | 100,000 (balancing charge) | CAA ss 61, 577 | **No** (not an exit charge provision) |
> | UK warehouse (bought GY1) | 3,000,000 | 3,800,000 | 800,000 **postponed** | TCGA ss 185, 187B | n/a (does not accrue now) |
> | £20m loan from TPLC (on demand) | 20,000,000 | 20,000,000 | nil | CTA 2009 s 333 | n/a |
>
> **CT computation, AP 1 January – 30 June GY4**
>
> | £ | CT1 (actual) | CT2 (ignoring exit provisions) |
> |---|---|---|
> | Trading profit | 1,200,000 | 1,200,000 |
> | Stock uplift on deemed cessation (s 162) | 300,000 | — |
> | Customer list realisation credit (s 859) | 1,200,000 | — |
> | Balancing charge (CAA) | 100,000 | 100,000 |
> | **Trading profits** | **2,800,000** | **1,300,000** |
> | Chargeable gain: Irish shares (s 185) | 600,000 | — |
> | Chargeable gain: warehouse (s 187B) | nil | nil |
> | **Taxable total profits** | **3,400,000** | **1,300,000** |
> | **CT at 25%** | **850,000** | **325,000** |
> | **Qualifying CT for a payment plan (CT1 − CT2)** | **525,000** | |
>
> Of the £325,000, £300,000 is tax on the ordinary trading profit and £25,000 on the balancing charge.
>
> **Instalments.** TIL is very large for this AP: the threshold is £20,000,000 ÷ 10 (QIP divisor for the 31 December companies in GY4: chapter 3) × 6/12 = **£1,000,000**, and its profits are £3,400,000. For a six-month AP ending on the last day of a month, HMRC's manual (CTM92815; chapter 3) puts instalments on **14 March** and **14 June GY4**. The sources checked for this book do not say how the instalment regime treats tax that is then deferred under a Sch 3ZB plan; a tax function would agree the position with HMRC as part of the s 109B arrangements.

Look at where the tax comes from. Only £325,000 relates to the ordinary trading profit and the balancing charge; £525,000 is tax on value never turned into cash. The stock is still on the shelves, the customer list is still in use, and the shares are unsold. That cash problem is the reason payment plans exist.

---

## Settling up before you go.

A company that has left the UK is hard to chase: its assets, directors and bank accounts may all be abroad. So TMA 1970 ss 109B–109F require a migrating company to settle its affairs **before** it leaves.

**Conditions A–D (s 109B), all to be met before the company ceases to be UK resident:**

| Condition | Requirement |
|---|---|
| A | Notice to HMRC of the company's intention to cease to be UK resident |
| B | The notice specifies the **migration time** |
| C | A **statement** of the tax payable for periods beginning before the migration time, with details of the **arrangements proposed for securing payment** (which may include a proposed CT exit charge payment plan) |
| D | Arrangements for securing payment **made and approved** by HMRC (disapplied to the extent payment is secured by a Sch 3ZB plan) |

Disputes over the amount in the statement go to the tribunal, whose decision is final; an approval is **void** if information was not fully disclosed.

**"Tax" (s 109F)** includes CT, PAYE and CIS deductions the company should have made, income tax deductible under ITA 2007 ss 946 and 966, and amounts under s 77C, with interest on all of them.

**Penalties and recovery:**

| Provision | Effect |
|---|---|
| s 109C | Company migrating without meeting A–D: penalty up to the **unpaid tax** for pre-migration periods |
| s 109D | Any person who knowingly takes part (directors; controlling companies and their directors) liable to a penalty of the same maximum; directors presumed party unless they show otherwise; professional advisers acting only as advisers excluded |
| s 109E | Tax unpaid **6 months** after it is payable (under the plan, if any): HMRC may, within **3 years** of a relevant time (broadly when the tax is finally determined, with a plan-based rule where a payment plan exists), serve notice on companies in the migrating company's **51% group** in the 12 months before migration and on **controlling directors** of the migrating company or of a company controlling it, who must pay within **30 days**; they may recover from the migrating company; the payment is not deductible |

So migration is a group event: TPLC and TEL would be first in line if TIL failed to pay.

> **Worked example 22.3: TIL's timetable (invented)**
>
> | Date | Step |
> |---|---|
> | 1 March GY4 | s 109B notice: intention to cease UK residence; migration time the end of 30 June GY4; statement of tax for periods to that date; proposed security: a Sch 3ZB plan for the qualifying CT, and the rest paid on the ordinary timetable with a TPLC guarantee for anything outstanding |
> | May GY4 | HMRC approves the arrangements (condition D) |
> | 14 March, 14 June GY4 | Instalments for the migration AP (very large company) |
> | End of 30 June GY4 | Migration time: board reconstituted in Dublin; AP ends; exit charges arise |
> | 1 July GY4 | New AP begins: TIL non-resident, within CT on its UK property business |
> | By 31 March GY5 | Last day to apply for the plan (within 9 months after the end of the migration AP) |
> | 1 April GY5 to 1 April GY10 | Six plan instalments of £87,500, plus interest |
> | By 30 June GY6 | Last day to elect out of s 187B (2 years after the deemed disposal); TIL does not elect |

---

## Paying over six years.

**TMA 1970 Sch 3ZB** (inserted by FA 2013 Sch 49; amended by FA 2019 Sch 8 Part 1, which replaced the old payment paragraphs 11–17 with a single six-instalment rule).

| Feature | Rule | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Eligible company | Has freedom of establishment under **TFEU Article 49** or **EEA Agreement Article 31**; ceases to be UK resident and becomes resident in a **relevant state** (an EU member state, or an EEA state with recovery assistance equivalent to Directive 2010/24/EU); carries on business there; not treaty-resident outside it | para 1 |
| Qualifying tax | **CT1 − CT2**: CT for the migration AP less CT computed ignoring the exit charge provisions (TCGA s 185; CTA 2009 s 162 via s 41(2)(b); s 333; s 609; s 859). Capital allowances are not on the list, so tax on a balancing charge is outside | para 2 |
| Application | Within **9 months** after the end of the migration AP, with the required details; security may be required where there is a serious risk to collection; void for non-disclosure | paras 1(4), 8 |
| Payment | **Six equal instalments**: the first on the day after the end of the 9 months following the migration AP; the others on the next **5 anniversaries** | para 11 |
| Interest | Runs as if there were no plan; late payment penalties only for missing plan dates | — |
| Acceleration | Whole balance due at the next instalment date on insolvency, administration, liquidation (or foreign equivalents), ceasing to be resident in a relevant state, or 12 months' non-payment; tax on a particular asset accelerated on its disposal (partly on a part disposal) | paras 12–14 |
| Realisation method | Removed for APs ending on or after 1 January 2020 (FA 2019 Sch 8 para 6(6)); CTM34133–CTM34134 still describe it and are out of date | — |

**Who can use it after Brexit?** **HMRC's view** (CTM34132) is that eligible companies are those **incorporated in an EU or EEA member state** that become resident in another such state. A UK-incorporated company no longer has Article 49 TFEU rights, so in practice it cannot use a plan (the book's reading of para 1 with CTM34132). The UK's own companies are shut out of a relief that still exists in UK law. legislation.gov.uk shows unapplied effects on Sch 3ZB; check the current text before relying on the detail.

> **Worked example 22.4: TIL's payment plan (invented)**
>
> TIL is incorporated in Ireland (an EU member state) and becomes resident in Ireland, where it carries on its business: an eligible company.
>
> | £ | |
> |---|---|
> | CT1 | 850,000 |
> | CT2 | (325,000) |
> | **Qualifying CT** | **525,000** |
> | Six equal instalments (525,000 ÷ 6) | **87,500** each |
> | Due dates | 1 April GY5, GY6, GY7, GY8, GY9 and GY10 |
> | Outside the plan: CT on the balancing charge (100,000 × 25%) | 25,000 |
>
> Interest runs on each instalment as if there were no plan. The plan defers the cash, not the cost of money.

> **Exam lens: notice, security and payment plans.**
> - **Grade:** within migration **2 (non-core)**.
> - **N25 Q3** rewarded: notice before migration (conditions A–D), the statement and security, penalties on company and directors, recovery from group companies, and the plan (eligibility, CT1 − CT2, 9 months, six equal annual instalments, interest, acceleration). The examiners found administration and plan detail weak.
> - **Traps:** treating the plan as a postponement of the charge (it defers payment; interest runs); applying it to a UK-incorporated company or a migration outside the EU/EEA; putting capital allowances balancing charges into CT1 − CT2; describing the realisation method; forgetting personal exposure of directors.

---

## After the move, and what the examiner looks for.

From 1 July GY4 TIL is a non-resident company. A new AP begins at once, because it remains within the charge to CT, but only on its UK property business (the warehouse rents) and, in time, on the warehouse gain including the postponed £800,000 (CTA 2009 s 5; TCGA s 2B; chapter 23).

| Regime | Effect of migration | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| Group relief | Without a UK PE, TIL can no longer surrender or claim | 15 |
| Gains group | TIL stays a member (non-resident companies count); no gain, no loss transfers only for assets within the UK charge | 17 |
| Transfer pricing | The £20m interest-free loan from TPLC no longer meets the UK-to-UK exemption (TIOPA 2010 s 164A): full Part 4 | 2, 27 |
| CFC rules | TIL becomes a CFC | 26 |
| SAO | No change (never in: Irish-incorporated) | 4 |

> **Going further: the tax function's migration project.**
> 1. **Months ahead:** test whether control will really move; rebuild the board; document the decision-making protocol.
> 2. **Valuation:** value every asset at the migration time (stock, intangibles, shares, plant, land, loans, derivatives); market values drive every exit.
> 3. **Model:** CT1, CT2, the plan, interest, and whether to elect out of s 187B within 2 years.
> 4. **Notice:** give s 109B notice, statement and proposals early enough for approval before the migration time; disclose fully (approval is void otherwise).
> 5. **Exposure:** brief directors on s 109D and the group on s 109E.
> 6. **Timing:** migrating when values are low reduces the exit charge; losses or reliefs available in the migration AP can absorb it.
> 7. **After:** register the new AP; set up transfer pricing documentation and the CFC review; update the group relief and gains group maps.
>
> **Ethics.** Residence can be argued either way on borderline facts. An adviser should not help a board "paper" a move of control that has not happened (*Development Securities*), and should make sure the s 109B statement discloses fully.

**How the examiner tests it.** Residence questions (N23 Q1; N24 Q6) reward applying incorporation, CMC, the supplied tie-breaker and s 18 to the facts at each date. Migration questions (N25 Q3) reward a full exit schedule, the land postponement and detailed administration. The trap runs both ways: in **M26 Q5** (a UK company's first overseas construction contract) many candidates wrongly discussed residence or migration of the UK company in a question about a foreign PE, and earned nothing for it. Answer the requirement asked.

---

## What to take away.

- **Residence:** UK incorporation (CTA 2009 s 14) or CMC in the UK. CMC is the highest level of control, usually the board acting as a board; a question of fact.
- **Boards:** influenced but deciding keeps control (*Wood v Holden* [2006]); bypassed loses it (*Unit Construction* [1960]); rubber-stamping uncommercial decisions really taken by the parent loses it (*Development Securities* [2020]).
- **Treaties:** a UK company cannot leave by moving its board; it is non-resident only if a treaty tie-breaker makes it resident elsewhere (s 18). Older treaties: POEM; MLI Article 4 (including UK–Ireland, from 1 April 2020 for UK CT): competent authority agreement. DRICs cannot surrender group relief or receive no gain, no loss transfers.
- **Exit:** the AP ends; TCGA s 185 deems disposal and reacquisition at market value of all assets except UK PE assets; s 187 postponement repealed (migrations from 1 January 2020); UK land postponed automatically under s 187B unless the company elects out within 2 years; stock (ss 41, 162), plant (balancing adjustments), intangibles (s 859), loans (s 333) and derivatives (s 609) all exit at market or fair value.
- **Before leaving:** notice, migration time, statement and approved security (TMA s 109B); penalties up to the unpaid tax (ss 109C–109D); recovery from 51% group companies and controlling directors (s 109E).
- **Plans:** an eligible company moving to an EU/EEA state pays CT1 − CT2 in six equal annual instalments with interest, applying within 9 months; in practice not available to UK-incorporated companies.
- **TIL:** TTP £3.4m; CT £850,000; plan £525,000 = 6 × £87,500 from 1 April GY5; warehouse gain £800,000 postponed.

So where does a company live? Where its mind is, unless it was born here. And how does it leave? Only by paying for what it takes with it.

TIL now has a UK foothold as a non-resident. Chapter 23, on inbound companies, permanent establishments and withholding, asks what the UK taxes when a foreign company does business here.

# Chapter twenty-three: Inbound: non-resident companies, permanent establishments and withholding

On 18 March 2026, Finance Act 2026 received Royal Assent. Buried in its Schedule 7 was a new sentence for the Corporation Tax Act 2010. It concerned the person who works in the UK for a foreign company. Under the old wording, that person created a taxable presence only if they had, and habitually exercised, "authority to do business on behalf of the company". Under the new wording, it is enough that they "habitually conclude contracts, or habitually play the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts that are routinely concluded without material modification by the company" (CTA 2010 s 1141(1)(b), as substituted by FA 2026 Sch 7).

Read that again slowly, because it is the heart of this chapter. A person who never signs anything can now give a foreign company a permanent establishment (PE) in the UK. The person who closes the deal matters more than the person who holds the pen.

This chapter is about companies that are not resident here but do business here. What does the UK tax them on? When does their activity here become a PE? How are profits attributed to it? Who answers for the tax? And, from the other side of the payment, when must a UK company deduct income tax from interest or royalties it pays to someone abroad? On the LCG grid, "company residence and chargeable profits of non-UK resident companies and concept of permanent establishment/branch", "non-resident and dual resident companies" (gains), CTA 2010 Part 22 (Chs 5–7 here) and "deduction of income tax" are all **core (grade 1)**. The chapter builds on *The Living Law* (TKS), chapter 26, which introduced residence, PEs and the branch.

Statutes: Corporation Tax Act 2009 (CTA 2009), Corporation Tax Act 2010 (CTA 2010), Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA 1992), Taxation (International and Other Provisions) Act 2010 (TIOPA 2010) and Income Tax Act 2007 (ITA 2007) Part 15. We apply the law for **FY2026**, and **2026/27** for income tax points.

---

## What the UK taxes on a foreign company

A UK-resident company pays corporation tax on its profits wherever they arise. A company resident elsewhere pays only where it has a link to the UK that the law recognises. Think of it as a footprint. The UK taxes a foreign company only where it has left a footprint here, and since 2026 the law also counts footprints made by others walking on its behalf.

**CTA 2009 s 5** lists the footprints. A non-UK resident company is within the charge to CT only if it:

| Head | Since |
|---|---|
| Carries on a trade of dealing in or developing UK land | 5 July 2016 (with CTA 2010 Part 8ZB) |
| Carries on a trade in the UK through a UK PE | long-standing (s 19) |
| Carries on a UK property business | **6 April 2020** (FA 2019 Sch 5) |
| Has other UK property income | 6 April 2020 |
| Loan relationship and derivative profits of that property business (s 5(3A)–(3B)) | 6 April 2020 |

Notice what is missing. A foreign company that sells to UK customers from abroad, with no PE here and no UK land, is not within CT on its trading profits at all. Trading **with** the UK is not trading **in** the UK through a PE.

For the PE head, **s 19 CTA 2009** charges the trading income arising directly or indirectly through or from the PE, plus income from property or rights used by or held by it, attributed under ss 20–24 (the cross-reference changed from "20 to 32" by FA 2026 Sch 7 for chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026). Land dealing and property income are charged under their own heads (s 19(2A)), not as PE profits.

**Gains** follow a parallel map in **TCGA 1992 s 2B**:

- **UK PE assets (s 2B(3)):** gains on assets situated in the UK, used for the PE's trade or held by it, attributable to the PE under CTA 2009 ss 20 and 24 (wording amended by FA 2026 Sch 7 para 28).
- **UK land (s 2B(4)):** since **6 April 2019**, gains on interests in UK land, whether or not the company has a PE.
- **Indirect disposals (s 2B(4), Sch 1A):** assets deriving **at least 75%** of their (gross) value from UK land ("UK property rich"), where the company has a **substantial indirect interest**. HMRC's manual explains that this means holding **at least 25%**, at some time in the **two years** before the disposal, with connected persons' interests attributed (CG73934, CG73936). There is a trading exemption where the land is used in a qualifying trade.
- **FA 2026 s 40:** each cell of a protected cell company is treated as a separate company for the Sch 1A 75% test, for disposals on or after 26 November 2025.

**In our invented case.** Tarnmoor plc is a listed engineering group; every company, person and number in it is invented for teaching. Two of its companies test the footprint rules in this chapter: **Tarnmoor Vallaria SA (TVS)**, resident in the invented country of Vallaria; and **Tarnmoor Ireland Ltd (TIL)**, which ceases to be UK resident on **30 June GY4** (chapter 22) but still owns a warehouse in England.

---

## A fixed place of business

**CTA 2010 s 1141(1)** gives two routes to a PE in a territory:

1. **(a) the fixed place limb:** "a fixed place of business there through which the business of the company is wholly or partly carried on"; and
2. **(b) the agent limb** (next section).

**s 1141(2)** lists fixed places: a place of management; a branch; an office; a factory; a workshop; an installation for exploring natural resources; a mine, well or quarry; and **a building site or construction or installation project**.

On the usual reading, three ideas sit inside "fixed place of business": a **place** (which may be modest, even floor space in someone else's premises); **fixed** (a link to a location with some permanence); and the company's **business carried on through it** (usually meaning the place is at the company's disposal and its business is done there). Since FA 2026, s 1140A directs that the PE chapter be read consistently with Article 5 of the OECD Model and its Commentary, so the Commentary's account of these ideas now shapes the UK reading.

**The domestic list sets no time limit for a building site.** Treaties usually do: under Article 5(3) of the OECD Model a building site or construction project is a PE only if it lasts **more than 12 months**. Under the domestic list, whether a short site is "fixed" is a question of degree (the book's reading: s 1141(2) contains no duration test). Where a treaty applies, its time limit protects the foreign company. In **M26 Q5** (20 marks) a construction PE turned on the 12-month test.

> **The subsidiary misconception.** A UK subsidiary is **not** a PE of its foreign parent merely because the parent controls it (HMRC, INTM153060, following the OECD Model). The subsidiary is a separate taxpayer. But a subsidiary **can** be the parent's dependent agent on the facts. Control alone proves nothing; conduct can prove a great deal.

> **And the examiners' complaint.** In **N25 Q2**, some candidates treated a PE as a separate legal entity. It is not. A PE is part of the foreign company: no shares, no directors, no separate legal personality. The law treats it *as if* it were a separate enterprise when attributing profits (s 21 CTA 2009), but that is a measuring hypothesis, not the law of persons.

---

## The agent who never signs

### Why the agent limb was rewritten

For decades, s 1141(1)(b) asked whether "an agent acting on behalf of the company has and habitually exercises there authority to do business on behalf of the company" (wording to 31 December 2025). In practice that pointed at the power to conclude contracts. Groups learned to live just outside it: a local company (often a group company) found the customer, negotiated the price and agreed the specification, then sent the contract abroad for signature. The foreign company signed; the local company earned a modest fee; the sales profit and the taxing right stayed abroad.

The international response came through the OECD/G20 base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS) project. The **Action 7** report (October 2015), "Preventing the Artificial Avoidance of Permanent Establishment Status", targeted commissionaire arrangements and similar strategies and proposed the "principal role" wording for Article 5(5), with a narrower independent agent exception in Article 5(6) (commentators' summaries; the OECD report was not opened: oecd.org is blocked). The UK's first answer was **unilateral**: the diverted profits tax (DPT) of 2015 had an "avoided PE" limb. DPT is repealed for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026 (chapter 30). The second answer is the new statutory wording, which brings the dependent agent test inside CT.

### The new test

For **chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026** (FA 2026 s 49, Sch 7 paras 12, 30), a company has a PE in a territory if:

> a person acting on behalf of the company in the territory **habitually concludes contracts**, or **habitually plays the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts that are routinely concluded without material modification by the company**,

and the contracts are:

- (i) for the **transfer of ownership of, or the granting of the right to use, property** owned by the company or that it has the right to use; or
- (ii) for the **provision of services** by the company.

| Phrase | What it asks |
|---|---|
| Acting on behalf of the company | Is the person doing the company's business rather than its own? |
| Habitually | Repeatedly, as a pattern, not once |
| Principal role | The role that actually closes the deal: persuading the customer, settling terms, agreeing price |
| Routinely concluded without material modification | Is the foreign company's signature a formality? If head office regularly rewrites deals, no; if it signs what arrives, yes |
| Contract types (i) and (ii) | Sales or licences of the company's property, or its services |

### Commencement (labelled real-calendar examples)

| Foreign company's year end | Period | Test |
|---|---|---|
| 31 December | 1 January 2025 – 31 December 2025 | Old wording |
| 31 December | from 1 January 2026 | **New** wording |
| 30 June | 1 July 2025 – 30 June 2026 | Old wording (began before 1 January 2026) |
| 30 June | from 1 July 2026 | **New** wording |

The same date governs the attribution rewrite (ss 20–21) and the closely related rule. The Tarnmoor story's periods are simply treated as falling under the new law.

### The purpose clause

**CTA 2010 s 1140A** (FA 2026 Sch 7 para 11) requires the PE chapter to be read consistently with Article 5 of the OECD Model Tax Convention and its Commentary as approved by the OECD Council on **18 November 2025**. So when you meet "principal role", the Commentary on that phrase is now part of how the UK statute is read (chapter 2). Whether s 1140A's reference is "as amended from time to time" (as ss 20 CTA 2009 and 164 TIOPA are) was not confirmed. **Proposed, not law:** the draft Finance Bill 2026-27 (13 July 2026) would amend s 1140A further as part of reform of the foreign PE exemption (chapter 2).

---

## Independent agents and the closely related rule

**s 1142(1) CTA 2010:** a company does not have a PE merely because it carries on business through an **agent of independent status acting in the ordinary course of its business**. A broker, general commission agent or freight forwarder serving many clients is the classic case.

**s 1142(1A)–(1B) (FA 2026 Sch 7 para 13):** a person is **not** of independent status if it is **closely related** to the company **and** acts **exclusively or almost exclusively** on behalf of the company (or it and other companies to which it is closely related). A group sales company working only for its sister companies cannot use the exception, however separate its board and books.

**"Closely related" (s 1143(2CA), replacing former (2D); FA 2026 Sch 7 para 14):** on all the relevant facts and circumstances, one person has control of the other, or both are under the control of the same person or persons; the definition also includes the 50% investment condition linked to TIOPA 2010 s 259ND. In a wholly owned group, every company is closely related to every other.

For agents outside the group, the usual factors still matter: legal and economic independence; whether the agent bears its own entrepreneurial risk; whether it acts for several principals; the degree of detailed instruction and control. A commission agent with fifty clients who loses money when sales fall is independent; a one-client agent whose diary is set by the principal looks dependent, group or no group.

**The common exam pattern.** A UK group company works almost entirely for a foreign group company. It cannot be independent. The only questions are whether it habitually concludes contracts, or plays the principal role leading to contracts routinely concluded without material modification, and whether a treaty prevents the charge.

---

## Preparatory, auxiliary and the fragmentation trap

**s 1143(1)–(3) CTA 2010:** no PE where the activities, **viewed in relation to the business as a whole**, are **only** of a preparatory or auxiliary character. Examples in the statute: facilities for storage, display or delivery of the company's goods; a stock of goods for storage, display or delivery, or for processing by another person; purchasing goods or collecting information for the company.

Two words carry the weight: "only" and "as a whole". An activity that is an essential and significant part of the company's business is not auxiliary even if it is on the list: a company whose business **is** warehousing cannot call its warehouse auxiliary.

**Anti-fragmentation (s 1143(2A)–(2C), added by FA 2019 s 21).** The exception does not apply where the activities carried on by the company, or by a closely related person, at the same place or at another place in the same territory, are **complementary functions that form part of a cohesive business operation**, and either:

- the **combination** of activities is not merely preparatory or auxiliary; or
- one of the places is already a PE of the company or of the closely related person.

> **Worked example 23.1 (labelled hypothetical, not story): a parts store**
>
> Suppose TVS rented a small unit near Leeds to hold spare valve parts for delivery to UK customers.
>
> | Step | Analysis |
> |---|---|
> | Fixed place? | Yes: a unit at TVS's disposal, through which part of its business (storage and delivery) is carried on |
> | Preparatory or auxiliary alone? | Storage and delivery of the company's goods are listed examples; on their own, auxiliary |
> | Anti-fragmentation? | Suppose TEL (closely related) services and repairs the same valves for the same customers. If store and servicing are complementary functions in one cohesive operation of supplying and maintaining the valves, and the combination is more than preparatory or auxiliary, the exception is lost |
> | Result | A fixed place PE of TVS (subject to any treaty) |

> **Exam lens: the PE definition**
> - **Grade:** company residence and chargeable profits of non-UK resident companies and concept of PE/branch, **core (1)**.
> - **Past appearances:** **N25 Q2** (15 marks, 6/9): PE analysis of four contracts (an independent agent, a preparatory or auxiliary activity, **anti-fragmentation**, a construction contract under 12 months) and the UK consequences of a PE. Examiners: few cited anti-fragmentation; some treated a PE as a separate legal entity. **N24 Q6** (10 marks): a non-UK company setting up in the UK (PE, CMC, residence, chargeability): very well answered when tied to the scenario. **M26 Q5** (20 marks): a construction PE abroad (the outbound mirror; chapter 25).
> - **Style:** technical prose, 0.5–1 mark per point; apply each limb to each fact.
> - **Traps:** treating a PE as a separate legal entity; forgetting anti-fragmentation where a group company works in the same country; applying the domestic test and stopping (check the supplied treaty); applying the 2026 wording to a period beginning before 1 January 2026; discussing residence or migration in a PE question (M26 Q5, N25 Q2).
> - **Check the 2027 grid** when published: FA 2026's rewrite makes this row likely to be examined.

## Domestic law meets the treaty

Most foreign companies trading here are resident in a treaty country. Where the two disagree, **the treaty wins**: TIOPA 2010 s 6 gives treaty arrangements effect, generally in priority to domestic law. Under **Article 7** of a treaty in OECD form, business profits of an enterprise of one state are taxable only there unless it carries on business in the other state through a PE situated there; and the treaty's own **Article 5** decides what a PE is. HMRC's manual: where a treaty applies, its PE article governs whether the UK may tax the business profits (INTM153060, INTM153080; see also INTM264200 on domestic law and treaty law).

The new domestic agent test can be **wider** than the treaty test. A treaty has the principal role wording only if the two states put it there, by a new treaty or through **Article 12 of the Multilateral Instrument (MLI)**. The UK did not take up Article 12: the HMRC synthesised text of the **UK–Ireland** treaty and MLI shows Article 12 does not apply there (**V**), and commentators report that the UK reserved on the whole article (**secondary**). So many UK treaties keep the older wording: an agent creates a PE only if it "has, and habitually exercises, an authority to conclude contracts in the name of the enterprise".

**The three-step routine.**

| Step | Question | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Domestic: fixed place or dependent agent; any exception (independent agent, preparatory or auxiliary, subject to anti-fragmentation)? | CTA 2010 ss 1141–1143 |
| 2 | Treaty: is there a PE under the treaty's Article 5? Use the **supplied extract**, not your memory of the Model | Treaty; TIOPA s 6 |
| 3 | The UK taxes business profits only if **both** answers are yes | Art 7 |

In **N23 Q1** the examiners noted that some candidates ignored the supplied treaty article and used the OECD Model text instead.

Where there is **no treaty**, step 1 is the whole answer. Marrovia (invented) has no UK treaty. A Marrovian company whose UK sister company habitually played the principal role in its sales would have a UK PE, full stop.

## Tarnmoor Vallaria's UK customers

**In our invented case (GY4).** TVS starts selling Ashlar valves directly to large UK water and energy utilities. The valves are made in Vallaria under the patent licence from Calder (chapter 11). TVS has no UK office, warehouse or staff. TEL's key-account engineers, based in Leeds, visit the customers, scope each job, propose the specification and negotiate the price. When the customer agrees, they send a completed contract to TVS's office in Vallaria, where it is signed. In the first six months nobody in Vallaria changes a commercial term. TVS pays TEL a service fee for the engineers' time, priced under the TP rules (chapter 27).

> **Worked example 23.2: Tom Hesketh's PE memo (GY4)**
>
> | Test | Facts | Conclusion |
> |---|---|---|
> | Fixed place (s 1141(1)(a)) | Leeds offices are TEL's, not at TVS's disposal | No |
> | Acting on behalf of TVS | Engineers sell TVS's valves | Yes |
> | Habitually | Every utility deal | Yes |
> | Principal role | Engineers settle specification and price | Yes |
> | Routinely concluded without material modification | TVS signs unchanged | Yes |
> | Contract type | Transfer of ownership of goods TVS owns | (i) met |
> | Independent agent (s 1142)? | TEL is closely related (common control by TPLC) and acts almost exclusively for the group in this market (s 1142(1A)) | Not independent |
> | **Domestic result** | | **UK PE of TVS (s 1141(1)(b))** |
> | Treaty Art 5 (invented UK–Vallaria treaty: older agent wording) | Engineers have no authority to conclude contracts in TVS's name; contracts signed in Vallaria | **No treaty PE** |
> | **Answer** | Art 7: UK may not tax TVS's business profits | **No UK CT for TVS** |

**Going further: why the board still changes the model.** A conclusion resting on a treaty is only as safe as the treaty and the facts. Treaties are renegotiated; facts drift (an engineer given signing authority, or contracts routinely signed in Leeds); a principal purpose test, where a treaty has one, can deny treaty benefits (chapter 24); and the board must consider how the arrangement looks in Vallaria and under the group's published tax strategy (chapter 4). **From 1 January GY5, TEL becomes a buy-sell distributor**: it buys Ashlar valves from TVS and sells to the utilities in its own name. That replaces a PE question with a TP question about the distributor's margin (chapter 27).

> **The misconception.** "A foreign company selling into the UK through a group company's sales team cannot have a UK PE, because the team works for a different company and nobody here signs." Before 2026 this was close to the truth. Since then the **principal role** test makes signing irrelevant, and the **closely related** rule makes the separate company irrelevant. Only a treaty with the older wording now stands between the foreign company and a UK charge.

**Going further: the tax function's checklist for inbound sales models.**

- Map every foreign group company selling into the UK and who does what: who finds, negotiates, prices, signs.
- **Contract conclusion protocols:** if the foreign company genuinely negotiates and modifies terms, document it; if it rubber-stamps, assume the domestic test is met.
- Choose the model deliberately: **buy-sell distributor** (UK profit in the UK company, TP on the margin), **service provider/agent** (PE risk under the 2026 test), **commissionaire** (the arrangement Action 7 targeted).
- Check each relevant treaty's Article 5 (older or newer agent wording; construction thresholds; any PPT).
- Revisit on any change of facts and at each year end; record conclusions in the TP records (chapter 27). Where a PE exists, a non-resident must notify chargeability and file returns.

## Attributing profit to a permanent establishment

Suppose the treaty had not protected TVS. What profit would the UK tax?

**CTA 2009 s 21** (as reworded by FA 2026 Sch 7 para 5): the profits the PE "might be expected to make" if it were "a separate and independent enterprise engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions", taking into account the **functions performed, assets used and risks assumed** through the PE and through the rest of the company. The PE is assumed to have the **same credit rating** as the company and the **equity and loan capital** it could reasonably be expected to have (s 21(2)).

**CTA 2009 s 20(1A)–(1E)** (substituted by FA 2026 Sch 7 para 4): ss 21 and 24 are to be read consistently with Article 7(2) of the OECD Model (approved 18 November 2025) and its Commentary, the **2010 Report on the Attribution of Profits to Permanent Establishments** (22 July 2010), the **Transfer Pricing Guidelines 2022** and the **March 2018 Additional Guidance**, as amended from time to time, subject to UK reservations, with a Treasury regulation power.

**The authorised OECD approach (AOA)**, as HMRC's manuals describe it (for example GIM10210; INTM450021 on PE records):

1. **Step 1: functional and factual analysis.** Hypothesise the PE as a separate enterprise; attribute functions, assets, risks and capital by reference to where the **people functions** that manage them are performed.
2. **Step 2: pricing.** Price the dealings between the PE and the rest of the enterprise at arm's length, applying TP methods by analogy.

> **Trap: repealed sections.** FA 2026 Sch 7 paras 6–8 **omitted CTA 2009 ss 22–23 and 25–32** for chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026: s 22 (transactions treated as arm's length), s 23 (goods and services provided to the PE), ss 25–28 (non-UK banks), **s 29 (allowable deductions)** and **ss 30–32 (restrictions, including s 32 on interest and financing costs)**. Citing "s 29" or "s 32" for a 2027 exam answer is quoting repealed law. s 24 remains.

**A live debate: dependent agent PEs.** One view: once the agent is paid an arm's length fee, nothing more is left for the PE. The other view, which commentators report the OECD's later work favours, looks at what the agent's people actually do: where they perform the functions that manage the enterprise's risks (inventory, credit, marketing intangibles), profit from those risks is attributed to the PE and the fee does not necessarily exhaust it. Outcomes range from nil to a large share of the sales profit. This is **disputed** territory internationally; the UK statute settles the method (s 21 read with the AOA), not the answer.

> **Worked example 23.3 (labelled illustration, not story)**
>
> | £ | |
> |---|---|
> | Profit attributed to the PE after the arm's length service fee to TEL (assumed) | 800,000 |
> | UK CT at 25% | **200,000** |
>
> TVS would then look to Vallaria for relief from double taxation under the treaty's elimination article (chapter 24). In practice the UK attribution and the TP pricing of TEL's fee must be consistent: chapter 27.

**Gains on PE assets.** Assets used for the PE's trade or held for the PE are within the CT charge on gains under TCGA s 2B(3), attributed under CTA 2009 ss 20 and 24.

**Coming from abroad.** HMRC's manual describes a compensating adjustment where a TP adjustment to a connected foreign company relates to a UK PE (INTM414510, reformed from 1 January 2026); the precise statutory route after FA 2026 was not located (flagged).

## Who answers for the foreign company

Taxing a company that lives abroad raises a practical problem: its directors, bank accounts and most assets are out of reach. **CTA 2010 Part 22** answers it in three short chapters, all core.

| Chapter | Sections | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Ch 6: UK representatives | ss 969–972 | A non-resident company's **UK PE is its UK representative**, treated as a separate person; the company's obligations on assessment, collection and recovery of CT are also the representative's (s 970); it remains the representative after the PE ceases, for tax relating to its period; limited exceptions (s 971) |
| Ch 7: recovery from related companies | ss 973–980 | If CT assessed on a **non-UK resident company** is unpaid **6 months** after it became payable, HMRC may serve a notice on a **related company** (a member of the same group, or of a consortium owning it, in the relevant period) requiring payment **within 30 days**; the notice has effect as an assessment; in consortium cases only a proportion (s 979); time limits in s 978 |
| Ch 5: set-off of income tax deductions | ss 967–968 | Income tax deducted from payments a company receives is set against its CT for the AP (s 967, UK resident; **s 968, non-UK resident**) |

**Do not confuse** Part 22 Ch 7 with **TMA 1970 ss 109B–109F** (chapter 22): the migration rules let HMRC recover unpaid exit tax from group companies and controlling directors at the moment of leaving. Ch 7 covers a company that is non-resident and remains chargeable here.

A non-resident within the charge (through a PE or a UK property business) is otherwise treated like any company for CT: it notifies chargeability, files returns, pays on the normal dates (by instalments if large) and is inside the regimes that apply to UK profits, such as the corporate interest restriction (chapter 28).

> **Exam lens: non-resident companies and Part 22**
> - **Grades:** chargeable profits of non-UK resident companies **1**; non-resident and dual resident companies (gains) **1**; Part 22 CTA 2010 (excluding Chs 3, 8 and ss 990–995) **1**.
> - **Past appearances:** **N24 Q6** (10 marks: when a non-resident company is chargeable, PE, CMC, residence; "very well answered"; higher marks for answers tied to the scenario).
> - **Traps:** saying a foreign company is taxed on all UK sales; forgetting that UK property income has been within CT since 6 April 2020; forgetting the 25%/2-year and 75% tests for indirect disposals; confusing Part 22 Ch 7 with the migration recovery rules.

## Why the payer collects the tax

Now turn the telescope around: a UK company is paying money to someone abroad. The logic of withholding is **collection**: a foreign lender is hard to assess; the UK payer is easy to find. So the payer deducts income tax at source and pays it to HMRC, and the recipient reclaims or credits it, or a treaty cuts it.

**ITA 2007 s 874:** a duty to deduct income tax from **yearly interest arising in the UK** paid by:

- a **company**, a local authority or a partnership with a company member; or
- **any person** to a person whose usual place of abode is outside the UK.

**Rate.** For **2026/27** the deduction is at the **basic rate, 20%** (s 874 ties the deduction to the basic rate for the tax year). **Coming next (enacted):** from **2027/28** the rate becomes "the savings basic rate" (FA 2026 s 6(8), Sch 1 para 29), set at **22%** for 2027/28 by FA 2026 s 5. s 874(6A): the location of the deed is ignored in deciding whether interest arises in the UK.

**Yearly or short?** No statute defines yearly interest. HMRC notes that tax law has distinguished yearly from short interest **since 1806** and that the line rests on case law (SAIM9075). Interest on a loan intended to last, or capable of lasting, a year or more is yearly (*Bebb v Bunny*); interest on a loan for less than a year with no provision to extend is short, despite an annual rate (*Goslings and Sharpe v Blake*, CA); mere failure to enforce a debt within a year does not make interest yearly (*Gateshead Corporation v Lumsden*). Intention at the outset matters most; HMRC wants clear evidence where short loans are repeatedly rolled over (SAIM9076; INTM413210 for series of short loans to non-residents).

> **The modern landmark.** *HMRC v Joint Administrators of Lehman Brothers International (Europe)* [2019] UKSC 12 (judgment 13 March 2019; on appeal from [2017] EWCA Civ 2124). The administration of LBIE (which began in 2008) produced a surplus after all proved debts, reported at around £7bn, much of it payable as **statutory interest** to creditors for the years they had waited. The Supreme Court held unanimously that this was **yearly interest** within s 874, so income tax had to be deducted. Interest compensating a creditor for being kept out of money over more than a year can be yearly even though it never accrued as a liability from year to year.

**Administration (ITA 2007 ss 945–962).** A UK-resident company accounts for tax deducted on "section 946 payments" (interest under s 874, royalties under ss 903 and 906, and others) on **form CT61**, for quarters ending **31 March, 30 June, 30 September and 31 December**, plus a short return period at the end of its AP. The return and the tax are due **within 14 days** after the end of the return period (ss 947, 949). The recipient sets the tax against its own liability (for a company, CTA 2010 ss 967–968).

## The exits from interest withholding

| Exit | Rule | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| **Excepted payments** | Beneficial owner is a **UK-resident company**; or a **non-UK resident company trading in the UK through a PE** that brings the interest into its chargeable profits; certain gross-paid bodies (local authorities, charities, pension scheme administrators) and partnerships of them | ITA 2007 ss 933–937 |
| **Reasonable belief** | The duty does not apply if the payer **reasonably believes** the payment is excepted; HMRC may direct otherwise (s 931) | ss 930–931 |
| **Banks** | Interest paid by a bank in the ordinary course of business; interest on an advance from a bank where the person beneficially entitled is within the CT charge on it | ss 878, 879 |
| **Quoted Eurobonds** | No deduction from interest on a quoted Eurobond: a security issued by a company, carrying a right to interest, **listed on a recognised stock exchange** or **admitted to trading on a multilateral trading facility operated by a regulated recognised stock exchange** (MTF limb from FA 2018; "regulated" from 31 December 2020) | ss 882, 987 |
| **Qualifying private placements** | Unlisted debt securities of a company meeting Treasury regulation conditions (in force 1 January 2016) | s 888A |
| **Treaty** | Lender claims on the **DT Company** form (relief at source or repayment, with certification of residence), or the borrower acts under an HMRC direction under the **Treaty Passport** scheme. **No self-help for interest** | TIOPA s 6; treaties |

**Treaty Passport.** A treaty-resident lender applies on **DTTP1**; a passport normally lasts **5 calendar years**. The UK borrower notifies each passported loan on **DTTP2** "as soon as possible". **Until HMRC issues a direction, the borrower must withhold** at the domestic rate.

**An exit that has closed.** The EU Interest and Royalties Directive exemptions (ITTOIA ss 757–767; ITA ss 914–917) were **repealed by FA 2021 s 34 for payments on or after 1 June 2021**. After Brexit, EU lenders need a treaty like everyone else.

> **Worked example 23.4: withholding across the Tarnmoor group (FY2026 rates; invented figures)**
>
> | Payment (annual) | Payer → payee | £ | Withholding? | Why |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Interest on £430m of loans at 6% (TEL £200m, TPLC £120m, TES £70m, TWS £40m) | UK companies → TFL | 25,800,000 | **None** | Excepted payment: beneficial owner a UK company (s 933) |
> | Interest on £550m 5.5% listed notes | TFL → bondholders | 30,250,000 | **None** | Quoted Eurobonds (s 882) |
> | (Counterfactual if unlisted, no treaty claims) | | | 20%: **6,050,000** | s 874 |
> | Project Undertow coupon on £80m 7% notes (rejected; chapter 29) | TFL → TCM (Marrovia: no treaty) | 5,600,000 | 20%: **1,120,000**; at 22% from 2027/28: **1,232,000** | s 874; no exit applies |
>
> TVS's interest to TFL (£7.2m) is paid by a Vallarian company: any withholding is Vallarian (10% under the invented treaty) and a DTR question for TFL (chapter 24), not a UK withholding point.

> **Going further: designing group debt for withholding.**
> - External bonds: list them (quoted Eurobond) or use a QPP.
> - Intra-group UK lending: excepted payments; keep the "reasonable belief" evidence (residence, beneficial ownership).
> - Overseas lenders: diarise DTTP2 filings and do not pay gross until HMRC's direction arrives; for non-passport lenders, the DT Company form.
> - Check whether interest is "yearly" on short facilities that are rolled over.
> - Withholding is rarely why a structure fails, but it is often the cost nobody costed. **M23 Q3** buried interest to **Bermuda** in a TP and CIR question; the examiners added that time was wasted on DPT, which does not apply to loan relationships.
